en: The Mahāvaipulya Triśaraṇa Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. And it was...

Mount Śailendra is lofty, steep, and vast, sustaining a multitude of various grains; it is like the great earth producing diverse kinds of flowers, a place where hosts of kinnaras and gandharvas constantly dwell and frequent, and where various multitudes—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—reside;
there are many kinds of diverse species, namely:
Lions, tigers, leopards, elephants, horses, qilin, bears, brown bears, deer, blue oxen, water buffaloes, rams, and monkeys—these various beasts dwell therein;
there are also immeasurable flocks of birds, namely:

peacocks, parrots, mynas, jīvañjīvaka birds, *kūṭa* birds, wild ducks, geese, ruddy sheldrakes, geese and ducks, black geese, mountain pheasants, *heji* birds, crows and pheasants, doves and pigeons, eagles and vultures, sparrows, and *cāṣa* birds—such birds as these rely upon it for their dwelling.
By the power of the Buddha, these sentient beings are not afflicted by greed, hatred, or delusion; they do not devour one another, but instead cherish each other as a mother loves her child.
At that time, within the king of mountains, the dense forests were lush and flourishing, with branches and twigs unbroken, abounding in various kinds of trees:

*devadāru* trees, *pīlu* trees, *aśvakarṇa* trees, *bhallāta* trees, *kiṃśuka* trees, *harītaka* trees, *āmalaka* trees, *bibhītaka* trees, *tāla* trees, *kaṇikāra* trees, *āmra* trees, *jambū* trees, *moca* trees, grapes, peaches, apricots, pears, *vilva* trees, walnuts, *aśmantaka* stones, *cūta* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, pines and cypresses, *prācīnāmalaka* trees, *paśya* trees, *kunkuma*, sandalwood, aloeswood, and storax; all such trees as these were present there without exception.
Within this king of mountains, all varieties of flowers of both water and land are fully present, namely:

*atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, *sumana* flowers, *śukandhara* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, *kaṇikāra* flowers, ox-hoof jasmine, hundred-petaled jasmine, and *mañjūṣaka* flowers. These various flowers are spread everywhere across its ground, adorning and illuminating the king of mountains.
Furthermore, there are water-blooming flowers—lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, and various other colors—all of which are fully present.
Within this king of mountains, at midnight, great clouds arise; from these subtle clouds of devas and nāgas, a fine rain of fragrant water with eight qualities descends.

In the time it takes for a single cow to be milked, this rain moistened Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; thereafter, the night became clear and bright, free from all clouds and mist, while a gentle breeze blew cool and refreshing, bringing joy to both body and mind.

The sentient beings dwelling within this king of mountains, as well as all the grasses and trees, became moistened and lustrous; just as when a flower garland is sprinkled with water, its radiant color becomes fresh and pure, increasing its excellence manifold.

On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa grow soft grasses, perfect in color, fragrance, and flavor; they are azure and curl to the right, possessing a myriad of exquisite hues like the neck of a peacock. Their fragrance is like that of the vārṣika flower, and their touch is like that of kāliṅga cloth. The ground is so soft that when one places the foot, it sinks four finger-widths, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state.

Within this king of mountains, there are many ponds and streams filled with clear, cool water, where various lotuses grow—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—in sizes as large as chariot wheels.
When flowers are gathered from it, their fragrance universally permeates an entire yojana.
At the summit of this king of mountains, there emerges a seat of great and wondrous lotuses—their stalks made of invincible blue lapis lazuli and their leaves of Jāmbūnada gold.
Its pedestal is made of solid black sandalwood, and its filaments are composed of the sovereign gem-king *musāragalva*.
It is as vast in length and breadth as the ocean, constantly upheld by ten billion *asura* kings.

It is covered above by nets of ten billion various-colored sovereign gems, while ten billion dragon kings rain down a shower of exquisite fragrances, and ten billion garuḍa kings [hover] with their mouths...
Holding silken banners and brocades, ten billion kinnara kings gazed upon him with joy;
ten billion mahoraga kings beheld him; ten billion gandharva kings sang praises and hymns;
ten billion celestial kings rained down powdered incense and garments, and rained down fragrant flowers, garlands, banners, pennants, and parasols; and ten billion Brahma kings likewise did so.
In the sky above, they stood in attendance with palms joined; ten billion devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens joined their palms in reverent salutation;
ten billion universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) with their retinues of the seven treasures arrived at his abode;
ten billion ocean-kings emerged from the great sea to pay him homage; and ten billion great jewel-king orbs provided illumination.
It was interspersed with billions of pure maṇi-jewel kings; it had billions of *pramoda* jewel kings as its flowers, fruits, and seeds;
it was illuminated by billions of *prabhāsa-guṇa* jewel kings and illuminated by billions of multicolored maṇi-jewel kings;
it was well-supported by *jambū-dhvaja* jewel kings, and [adorned] with billions of golds.
The great lotus, which possesses the indestructible adornment of the king of jewels, the firm lion; the variegated adornment of ten billion sun-treasury kings of jewels;
the emergence of various colors from ten billion inconceivable kings of multicolored jewels;
and the manifestation of inexhaustible adornments from ten billion wish-fulfilling kings of jewels—this great lotus has emerged from the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Born from the roots of goodness, sustained by the resolve of Bodhisattvas, and manifesting throughout all directions;
arising from the karma of wholesome dharmas produced by the illusion-like nature of reality; adorned by the eye of the dharma of non-contention, born from the nature of dreams;
originating from non-action and coming from the unimpeded path, it pervades and fills the ten [directions].
The Dharma-realm is brought about by the merit of the Buddha’s sphere;
even if one were to praise its merits for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they could never be exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon this flower, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, whose names were as follows:

Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Udāyin, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Subāhu, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Kātyāyana, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Aniruddha, Subhūti, Revata, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Rāhula, Nanda, and the Venerable Ānanda, and others like them.

Thus, these eight thousand foremost ones were all together; they had thoroughly realized the nature of reality as it truly is, observed the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), transcended the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and crossed the ocean of existence. They practiced the space-like conduct of the Tathāgatas, forever severed their bonds, and were free from the obstructions of a nest or dwelling. They moved in emptiness and tranquility, forever cut through the net of doubt, and placed their faith in the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom. Having reached the further shore, they benefited and brought profit to the world, acting as uninvited friends. Desiring to protect all sentient beings, they never abandoned any being with a heart of compassion. They were well able to manifest all the practices of the Buddhas, guarding the Buddha-dharma and vowing to protect the Buddha-dharma. Skillfully entering the lineage of the Buddhas, they were directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Furthermore, there were eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together,
with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī as their leaders, including Anuttarajñāna Bodhisattva, Anuttararatnajñāna Bodhisattva,
Asaṅgajñāna Bodhisattva, Puṣpadhvajajñāna Bodhisattva, Sūryadhvajajñāna Bodhisattva, and Candradhvajajñāna Bodhisattva.
Jñāna Bodhisattva, Vimalottara-jñāna Bodhisattva, Vajra-jñāna Bodhisattva, Vigataraja-jñāna Bodhisattva,
Samantabhāṣa-jñāna Bodhisattva, Prabhā-ketu Bodhisattva, Parvata-ketu Bodhisattva,
Ratna-ketu Bodhisattva, Asaṅga-ketu Bodhisattva, Puṣpa-ketu Bodhisattva, and Viśuddha-ketu Bodhisattva.
Sūryadhvaja Bodhisattva, Kāmaratidhvaja Bodhisattva, Vimaladhvaja Bodhisattva,
Samantaprasādadhvaja Bodhisattva, Bhūmistejas Bodhisattva, Ratnastejas Bodhisattva, Mahātejas Bodhisattva,
Vajrajñānatejas Bodhisattva, Vimalatejas Bodhisattva, and Sūryatejas Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Moon Splendor, Bodhisattva Mountain Splendor, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Illumination Splendor,
Bodhisattva Universal Splendor, Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, and Bodhisattva Viśuddhaguṇagarbha.
Dharmasāgaragarbha Bodhisattva, Samantaprasādagarbha Bodhisattva, Nāvāgarbha Bodhisattva, Padmaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva,
Sūryanetra Bodhisattva, Viśuddhanetra Bodhisattva, Vimalanetra Bodhisattva, Apratihatanetra Bodhisattva,
Samantadarśinetrabodhisattva, Suśreyasprajñānetra Bodhisattva, and Suvarṇa... [Bodhisattva].
Vajranetra Bodhisattva, Ratnanetra Bodhisattva, Gagananetra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Devamakuṭa Bodhisattva,
Dharmadhātuvyūhamānamakuṭa Bodhisattva, Maṇiratnamaṇḍalamakuṭa Bodhisattva, Sarvadigabhirāmamakuṭa Bodhisattva, Sarvabuddhapratyakṣakośamakuṭa Bodhisattva, and Ekātikrānta Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Universal Crown of All Worlds, the Bodhisattva Universal Delight Crown, the Bodhisattva Undestroyed Crown,
the Bodhisattva Crown Covering the Lion Thrones of All Tathāgatas, the Bodhisattva Crown Illuminating the Space of the Entire Dharma Realm,
the Bodhisattva Dragon Lord Topknot, the Bodhisattva Brahma Lord Topknot, and the Bodhisattva Free from All Buddhas...
Dharmamānaveśa Bodhisattva, Maṇicūḍa Bodhisattva, Sarvapraṇidhānasāgarasvaranirghoṣamaṇicūḍa Bodhisattva,
Sarvatathāgataprabhāmaṇḍalamaṇicūḍa Bodhisattva, Sarvākāśāsaṃbhedyavāgbharaṇamaṇicūḍa Bodhisattva,
and Sarvabuddharddhivyūhapradyotadhvajamaṇijālasaṃchāditacūḍa Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sarva-tathāgata-dharma-śāstra-nirghoṣa-śikhaṇḍin,
the Bodhisattva Sarva-triyadhva-nāma-śabda-śikhaṇḍin, Mahāprabha, Viśuddhaprabha, Ratnaprabha, Vimalaprabha, Candraprabha, Dharmaprabha, and Śāntiprabha.
...Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, Bodhisattva Abhijñāprabha, Bodhisattva Devaprabha, Bodhisattva Guṇalakṣaṇa,
Bodhisattva Jñānalakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Dharmalakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Abhedyalakṣaṇa,
Bodhisattva Prabhālakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Puṣpalakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Maṇilakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Buddhākāra, and Bodhisattva Brahmākāra.
The Bodhisattva Universal Transcendence, the Bodhisattva Brahma-Sound, the Bodhisattva Ocean-Sound, the Bodhisattva Earth-Sound,
the Bodhisattva World-Sound, the Bodhisattva Stone-Mountain-Sound, the Bodhisattva Sound Pervading the Dharma-Dhātu,
the Bodhisattva Thunder-Sound of the Ocean of All Dharmas, and the Bodhisattva Sound that Shatters the Battle-Fields of All Māras.
...the Bodhisattva Thunder-Sound of Great Compassion, the Bodhisattva Sound that Extinguishes All Worldly Suffering and Affliction,
the Bodhisattva Dharma-Vīra, the Bodhisattva Vṛddhi-Vīra, the Bodhisattva Jñāna-Vīra, the Bodhisattva Guṇa-Śaila-Vīra,
the Bodhisattva Guṇavardhana-Vīra, the Bodhisattva Yaśas-Vīra, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha-Vīra, and Mahā...
Maitreya-vīrya Bodhisattva, Jñānaprakāśa-vīrya Bodhisattva, Tathāgata-gotra-vīrya Bodhisattva,
Prabhāśrī Bodhisattva, Vijayaśrī Bodhisattva, Dharmavīryaśrī Bodhisattva, Samantaprabhāśrī Bodhisattva,
Dharmaśrī Bodhisattva, Candraśrī Bodhisattva, Gaganasrī Bodhisattva, Ratnaśrī Bodhisattva...
Bodhisattva Śānta, Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇaguṇa, Bodhisattva Jñānaguṇa, Bodhisattva Brahmarājaguṇa,
Bodhisattva Dharmādhipatirāja, Bodhisattva Lokādhipatirāja, Bodhisattva Brahmādhipatirāja, Bodhisattva Śailaparvateśvararāja,
Bodhisattva Gaṇādhipatirāja, Bodhisattva Devādhipatirāja, and Bodhisattva Śāntyadhipatirāja.
The Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhidharaṇīnirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Acalendrarāja, the Bodhisattva Nirmāṇendrarāja,
the Bodhisattva Bodhivikrāmindrarāja, the Bodhisattva Śāntanirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇanirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Pṛthivīnirghoṣa,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsāgaranirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Meghanirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Dharmāvabhāsanirghoṣa, and the Bodhisattva Gagananirghoṣa.
Bodhisattva Sarvasvara, Bodhisattva Suvilocanaghoṣa, Bodhisattva Prasthānapūrvapraṇidhānaghoṣa,
Bodhisattva Sarvamāramaṇḍalavikiraṇabuddhi, Bodhisattva Jñānaparvatabuddhi, Bodhisattva Gaganabuddhi, Bodhisattva Asaṅgabuddhi,
Bodhisattva Pratibodhanirghoṣabuddhi, and Bodhisattva Tryadhvāvabhāsabuddhi.
Together with eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, including the bodhisattvas Sāgarabuddhi, Ratnabuddhi, Abhayabuddhi, Samantāvabhāsabuddhi, and Dharmadhātucakṣuravabhāsabuddhi—
all of whom were fully endowed with the vows and practices of Samantabhadra, whose conduct was unimpeded, and who manifested [their presence] throughout all buddha-fields— [the assembly gathered].
Measuring their own bodies, they are able to go to the presence of all Buddhas;
their visual faculty is pure, and what they see is immeasurable, such that they can manifest as Buddhas;
the objects of all their supernormal powers are immeasurable, and wherever there is a place where any Tathāgata attained enlightenment, they go to all those places without ever becoming weary.
The light of wisdom universally illumines the ocean of all dharmas; even after immeasurable billions of kalpas, one could never exhaust the praise of its virtues.

Its eloquence in teaching is pure and equal in measure to space; its wise conduct is pure and free from any dependence. It manifests forms according to the inclinations of sentient beings without any obstruction; it understands the non-existence of sentient beings and the realm of selflessness. Its wisdom is like space, like a net of the light of wisdom that universally illumines the entire dharma-realm.

Their minds are ultimately tranquil and undisturbed; they possess the realm of the seeds of wisdom for all *dhāraṇīs*, and they proceed without obstruction through the *samādhis* and fearlessnesses. Abiding within the *dharmadhātu* with billions of eyes, they practice all dharmas and attain fearlessness. They contemplate the immeasurable ocean of wisdom, reach the further shore of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and attain the *prajñā-pāramitā* and the *abhijñā-pāramitā*. Having transcended all worldly *samādhi-pāramitās*, they have attained perfect mastery.

Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, headed by the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā, the bhikṣuṇī Padmā, the bhikṣuṇī Gautamī of Extreme Austerity, and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula; these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were together with them as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were five hundred upāsakas, whose names were:

the upāsaka Suvīryaśrī, the upāsaka Devavīryaśrī, the upāsaka Prajñāprabha, the upāsaka Yaśovīryaśrī, the upāsaka Atiyaśovīryaśrī, the upāsaka Sumati, the upāsaka Candravīrya, the upāsaka Candraprīta, the upāsaka Mahāprīta, the upāsaka Rāhubhadra, and the upāsaka Mahābhadra—these were the five hundred upāsakas, headed by such as these.

Furthermore, there were five hundred upāsikās, headed by the upāsikā Mahāprabhā, the upāsikā Suprabhā, the upāsikā Sukāya, the upāsikā Rucitakāya, the upāsikā Bhadrā, the upāsikā Bhadraguṇā, the upāsikā Candraprabhā, the upāsikā Lakṣaṇaprabhā, the upāsikā Guṇaprabhā, and the upāsikā Sunetra—these were the five hundred upāsikās who served as their leaders.
And other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, respectfully surrounded the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the Dharma, entitled "The Three Precepts. He extensively analyzed and explained the realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas and the practices of Bodhisattvas; it was able to universally illumine the entire Dharma-realm and clearly shine upon all fields of the Dharma-realm. It entered into the pure adornment of all Dharma-realms, annihilated all heterodox paths, and subdued all Māras and enemies. It brought universal joy to all realms of sentient beings, was able to know the deluded minds of all sentient beings, and preached according to their mental dispositions. It skillfully illuminated and transformed the faculties of sentient beings, manifesting them for their benefit.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-dharma, the [ten] powers, and the fearlessnesses, what dharmas should such persons gather?
By what dharmas should one protect these sentient beings?
"By what Dharma should one ensure that they do not regress from the unsurpassed, true path?
Having thus requested, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kāśyapa! What you have now asked brings great peace, happiness, and security to the world, and benefits both devas and humans; it is well that you are able to ask the Buddha about such a matter.
Kāśyapa! Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it to you in detail.
The Venerable Kāśyapa and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Kāśyapa, if there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha’s wisdom, the Buddha’s powers, and the fearlessnesses..."
These sentient beings, regarding all phenomena, should realize there is nothing to be attained and nothing to rely upon, thereby giving rise to various roots of goodness. Kāśyapa!

If there is a bodhisattva seeking the unsurpassed, right, and true path who becomes attached to signs—whether conceiving the Buddha-dharma as having conditioned characteristics, or conceiving the Buddha-dharma as having unconditioned characteristics, or conceiving the Buddha-dharma as having false characteristics—and who, having created such characteristics for themselves, thinks "I know the Buddha-dharma," and stubbornly clings to these characteristics without relinquishing them, one should say that this person is not called one who is heading toward the unsurpassed path.
Why is this? To desire the Buddha-dharma is itself to be attached to a self; one should practice in this way.
If one repeatedly clings to a self, one will be unable to sever it.
If one cannot sever [these], there will be longing; that which is the object of longing is the dharma of longing, and one is thereby harmed.
If one is harmed, one gives rise to restless wandering;
if one gives rise to restless wandering, there is cyclic existence.
If there is already transmigration, then there is penetration;
if there is already penetration, then there is false conceptualization;
if there is already false conceptualization, then there is discrimination.
If one has already engaged in discrimination, one increases false conceptualization;
if one increases false conceptualization, then there is discursive thought;
if there is discursive thought, then there is firm attachment.
If one is firmly attached, then there is pursuit;
if there is pursuit, then there is delusion;
if one is already deluded, then one has lost [the way].
What is loss? It is the loss of peace and security.
What is peace and security?
This refers to non-conceptualization.
If conceptualization arises, then there is permanence;
if there is permanence, then there is obstruction.
If there is obstruction, then there is abiding;
if there is abiding, then there is continuity;
if there is continuity, then there is contradiction.
If there is already contradiction, then there is further contradiction;
if there is further contradiction, then there is error;
if there is already error, then there is madness.
If one is already deranged, there is deception;
if one is already deceptive, there is distress;
if one is already distressed, there is regret.
If one has already given rise to regret, then harm ensues; one becomes attached to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas according to what one cherishes.
Yet, in reality, there is no fixed dharma to which one can be attached; it is merely through the shifting of perceptions that one is bound by perception—this is called the "bond of perception."

Greed has no fixed location, hatred has no fixed location, and delusion has no fixed location; arising from a mind of false conceptualization and discrimination, one is unable to cross over to the unsurpassed right path.
Kāśyapa! This is called a locus of craving.
Why is it named a locus of craving?

There is no fixed dharma that can be called craving; there is no dharma that is craved, nor any object of craving. Yet one is firmly attached to craving—merely empty attachment—namely, attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, and attachment to the pure and the impure.

Kāśyapa! All phenomena are empty; it is through false conceptualization that they are taken as objects. If there were no objects, the very notion of "object" would not exist; yet if one takes *bodhi* as an object, then this is the notion of a self (*ātman*).
If one possesses the notion of a self, they cannot be called a bodhisattva!
Why is it called the "notion of a self"?
Although there is that which is conceived, the conception itself is unobtainable.
To conceive of non-attainment is called the "notion of self.
Therefore, this unreal phrase is termed the "notion of self.
If sentient beings were real, then awakening would be real.
What is bodhi? It is the vision that all phenomena are entirely like illusions.
In what way are they like illusions?
This means that one does not speak of the notion of a self, the notion of a life-force, or the notion of a sentient being.
If there is the notion of existence or non-existence in the mind, such a person is attached to both notion and non-notion;
if they are attached to notion and non-notion, they are thereby crazed and intoxicated.
If one is already intoxicated with madness, then one is pursued by all manner of sufferings;
if one is pursued by all manner of sufferings, the Tathāgata says that such a person is said to dwell in madness and deceit.
Why is it called flattery?
Because one dwells in delusion and possesses false conceptualization;
if there is false conceptualization, then there is the notion of "I" and "mine."
If there were "self" and "what belongs to self," then there would be verbal expression;

if there were verbal expression, the Tathāgata says that such is called "non-expression. That [verbal expression] is held by verbal expression; therefore it is said that all dharmas arise from conceptualization, and all are my true reality.
“Kāśyapa! It is just as when a mass of clouds arises in the sky, yet that mass of clouds does not come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.”

The Tathāgata speaks truthfully that he does not come from any of the ten directions or locations; having understood this, he speaks according to reality, expounds in accordance with the meaning, and teaches with words that correspond to the truth.
Yet this gathering of clouds is not actually a gathering; it is designated as a "gathering of clouds.
Why is it called a "gathering of clouds"?
Because it gives rise to a multitude of variegated colors—various and diverse colors arising from falsehood—and because within it there is no fixed nature, it is called mist and clouds.
Seeing clouds and mist arise, although one sees them, there is no fixed perception of them; therein, clouds and mist ultimately have no reality.
"Kāśyapa! It is just as if someone were to say to another person:
"Let us go together to sit in the shade.
A person of wisdom speaks thus:
"I will not go now."
The person replied: "I do not say that there is a self; I only say that there are aggregates (skandhas).
As the wise have said:"
“If you speak of the aggregates, then they are not aggregates.
“Kāśyapa! Observe this person: even toward a few words of discourse, he remains unattached.”
In this way, Kāśyapa!
Those who understand the path of the Tathāgata’s dharma-nature roar the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly. Kāśyapa!

The Tathāgata still desires to practice wholesome dharmas regarding unwholesome dharmas; if sentient beings in the world possess the notion of a self, they are, in the presence of the Tathāgata, [regarded as] the ultimate truth.

Why is this? Because for the Tathāgata, such a notion of "self" is understood as being no-notion at all; yet other petty ordinary beings, not understanding that the Tathāgata speaks according to what is appropriate, contend with the Tathāgata.
Therefore, I say that the world disputes with me, but I do not dispute with the world.
What is meant by "the world"?
The world refers to sentient beings.
What is called the world of sentient beings?
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands that the world is suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is named the world of sentient beings.
All ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to this cognition of their own accord:
"This arises" and "this ceases"—they thus harm one another.
This is their discourse intended to transcend the world. Why is this?
This results in great darkness because one dwells in attachment to the world.

If one dwells in attachment to the world, there is greed; if there is greed, there is hatred; if there is hatred, there is delusion; if there is delusion, there is contention; and if there is contention, there is conflict.
With whom is one in conflict? It is with the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas. If one is in conflict, there is craving; if there is craving, there is grave conflict;

if there is grave conflict, one grasps at existence (*bhava*); if one grasps at existence, one seeks existence; if one has already sought existence, one knows no contentment; if one knows no contentment, one acts excessively; if one acts excessively, there is much desire; if there is much desire, one dwells in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; if one dwells in the three realms, one becomes attached; if one is already attached, there is no turning back the stream (*anuloma*); if there is no turning back the stream, one constantly undergoes death; if one constantly undergoes death, one does not reach Nirvāṇa; if one does not reach Nirvāṇa, one reaches that which is impossible to reach—that is, one reaches hell.

Thus it is, Kāśyapa! To practice what is inauspicious is called non-cultivation. If one does not cultivate correctly, there will be anger; if there is anger, there is no seeking; if there is no seeking, one does not recognize the notion of "I"; and if one does not recognize the notion of "I," one becomes of one heap and one substance with that which is called "I" and "mine."
What is meant by "self"?
It is to cling to what is unreal, to give rise to various false imaginings, and to perform various karmas.
If one gives rise to various false imaginings and performs various karmas, then one is attached to a self.
What is "mine"? Because there is no wisdom, it is called "mine.
Furthermore, as for this body, the aggregation of various phenomena is termed a "body," and it is called the fruit of the aggregate of precepts.

To treat others with contempt due to a mind of anger, and because of that anger, to give rise to the conceit of "I am," just as one gathers, receives, and guards a heap of growing grain—this is called "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*).

If there is the notion of "mine," then there is delusion; if there is delusion, then there is ignorance; if there is already ignorance, then there is slander; if there is slander, then there is anger; if there is already anger, then there is grasping, and one is thereby consumed by fire.

That which is burned is burned by perceptions—namely, the perception of a man, the perception of a woman, and the perception of a life-force; this is what I accept as "mine. This is called "what belongs to me" (*mamāyita*).
Those who possess "mine" revile what is "mine.
To revile what is "mine" means they are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); they are those who rely upon the path of ordinary persons, and this is called "mine."
“Kāśyapa! If one does not hear this Dharma, yet knows awakening and knows the bodhisattva practices—this is knowing through practice. Kāśyapa!”
This bodhisattva practice is entirely without practice; it is called "bodhisattva practice.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, that the bodhisattva practice is fulfilled, certain, and utterly pure—such a thing is impossible.
If there is one who is diligent and expounds this Great Dharma, it is because they regard all phenomena as being like a collection of space, not grasping at a collection of phenomena.

What this person speaks accords with the Great Dharma and is not discordant; such a person possesses merit and does not dwell in evil states. This is virtuous conduct that is yet non-conduct; such a person is able to uphold the Dharma, and thus receives and maintains it without attachment to the upholding of the Dharma.
Why is this? That which is spoken by the Tathāgata is the most supreme, the foremost among those worthy of offerings.
When sentient beings inquire about the Path, I ought to answer them with the sublime Dharma.
What is the supreme dharma?
It is that all dharmas are without conceptualization. "Kāśyapa!..."
In this way, a bodhisattva is said to maintain pure precepts: their mind does not give rise to evil,
they do not create obstacles, they do not slander bhikṣuṇīs, they do not associate with laypeople, and they refrain from killing,
stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and from covetousness or malice.
He does not hold wrong views; he does not afflict himself nor afflict others; he does not associate with sensual desires, nor does he covet sensual pleasures;
he does not revile, nor does he engage in frivolous jesting; he neither acts himself nor instructs others to act [in such ways];
he does not go to brothels, nor to the homes of widows, nor to those of young maidens, nor does he approach bird-catchers.
They do not associate with fishermen or hunters, nor with executioners, *caṇḍālas*, or those who covet the wives of others or drink liquor;
they do not even take such people’s hands in their own or engage in disputes with them, avoiding them just as one would avoid a vicious dog. It is the same regarding these [other types of persons].

Having abandoned and distanced oneself from these matters, one does not give rise to even a single thought of an evil mind; dwelling instead in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one abandons twenty things.

What are these twenty? One abandons women and never plays with them or speaks coarse words to them; one does not engage in debate or provoke quarrels and disputes; one abandons failing to respect and make offerings to one’s parents; and one abandons failing to respect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If there are fewer than twenty nuns, one should not preach the Dharma, except when men are present.

If a bhikṣuṇī is assembled for a Dharma discourse, he should not go to her place; he should never inquire after her welfare, nor write letters for women, nor compose them on their behalf. He should not accept invitations from relatives, nor ever allow his mind to dwell before a woman with desire, nor even travel along the same road as her.

If there is a bhikṣuṇī who mocks another and does not respond in kind, she shall never at any time accept or wear the robes of a bhikṣuṇī, except when robes are offered by someone while she is preaching the Dharma before the fourfold assembly; even then, she should generate a mind like the earth and only thereafter accept them, but not receive them face-to-face.
At all times, if a bhikṣuṇī should urge him to accept robes as an offering, he shall never accept them.
At all times, even if he is suffering from illness, if a bhikṣuṇī should urge him to eat, he shall never eat it, much less when he is not ill.
At all times, when widows invite him for a meal, he will never accept it if the number of monks is incomplete.
At all times, he does not enter the nuns' quarters;
nor does he ever respond to invitations from nuns, but rather stands with arms folded, looks up, and turns his back to walk away.

When the Dharma is being preached, if there is a bhikṣuṇī who comes to prostrate at one’s feet, joining her palms with a sincere heart, not looking away, and not moving her feet—this is not what constitutes physical strength or being called a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa).
If the mind is courageous and steadfast, fixing right mindfulness on a single point, this is what is called a "man."
One should not give rise to attachment toward any object, nor should one ever give rise to anger at any time; one should always maintain focused mindfulness upon omniscience.
Having heard this Dharma, one should practice and train in it so as to increase it.

“Kāśyapa! If those sons and daughters of good family who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle, having heard the Dharma, are unable to practice and study it, they will ultimately never attain the unsurpassed right path.”
For what reason? Kāśyapa!
It is by means of cultivation and study that one attains the unsurpassed path; it is not through the absence of cultivation and study that one attains the unsurpassed path.
Kāśyapa! If one could attain the unsurpassed path without practicing and training, then even rabbits, horses, cats, and mongooses would likewise attain the unsurpassed path. Why is this?
"One who acts improperly has no awakening.
"Kāśyapa! If one were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of sound, one would say as follows:"
"If I shall become a Buddha!
I shall become a Buddha!"—
then those infinite sentient beings would likewise have to become Buddhas.

Kāśyapa! It is difficult for sentient beings even to possess such practice; they cannot even maintain it with single-minded devotion for a single day and night, let alone for one kalpa or even a thousand kalpas. Therefore, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is exceedingly rare.

“Kāśyapa! Suppose all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to sing with one voice for one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand kalpas, or even ten trillion kalpas, saying:
‘All sentient beings, you shall become Buddhas!’”
"You shall become a Buddha!
Thus these people, being untiring in this way, constantly say:
"You shall become a Buddha!"
"You shall become a Buddha!
Even with such verbal exertion, he could not cause them to give rise to the bodhicitta; that they would attain Buddhahood is impossible.

“Kāśyapa! After my parinirvāṇa, during the final age, and after you and the others have entered parinirvāṇa, when the devas no longer provide protection, there may be those who hear what I have taught and resolve their minds on bodhi, and there may be bhikṣus who resolve their minds on bodhi; they should abide by twenty dharmas.”
What are these twenty? They are:
associating with bhikṣuṇīs; consuming impure food; being attached to morsel food; and accepting food recommended by bhikṣuṇīs. Kāśyapa!
"Just as today a learned bhikṣu, whether in a secluded and quiet place or within a great assembly, diligently cultivates and gathers the Dharma;
so it shall be, Kāśyapa!

At that time, those bhikṣus, whether in a village or in a secluded place, will gather together with bhikṣuṇīs and diligently inquire about the Dharma, yet they will give rise again to thoughts of sensual desire rather than thoughts of the Dharma."
This bhikṣuṇī gives rise to much desire in her mind and little to the Dharma-mind.
Kāśyapa! You should observe that such a person, though bearing the name of one who has attained bodhi, shall fall into the great, evil, and terrifying paths.

“Kāśyapa! Observe how at that time they feign the Dharma to associate with one another; when they meet, they speak impure words, burning with the fire of desire; when they associate, they take one another as disciples, first bowing in salutation according to the teacher-disciple dharma, but from then on they gradually dispatch messengers;
when they dispatch messengers, they seek out those of superior reputation.”
Once her name was known, he took her as his private wife, and they entered and exited together along the path.
Later, he heard others ask:
"To whom does she belong?"
How is it that kinsmen address one another as sisters and meet repeatedly?
Because they meet repeatedly, they fall into improper conduct, giving rise to lustful thoughts toward one another, and gradually manifest signs of desire.

By speaking thus, they have committed impure conduct and practiced the ways of King Yama; they have lost the path to bodhi, rebirth in heaven, and nirvana; they have abandoned the Tathāgata and forsaken the Dharma, and there is likewise no benefit for the Saṃgha.

Dwelling in one place, they give rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of malice, and thoughts of harm; such persons lack the bodhisattva’s practice and the four pure brahma-vihāras. Just as other bodhisattvas diligently cultivate the four brahma-vihāras, so too do these persons diligently cultivate thoughts of desire, ill will, and the like.
“Kāśyapa! At that time, there will be those who dwell as evil persons; there will be those who dwell as thieves; and there will be those who dwell in strife and contention. Kāśyapa!”

At that time, when all restraints have been utterly destroyed, upon hearing such sutras as these, they will give rise to contempt and disparagement; yet regarding the precepts they originally upheld and the acts of giving they originally practiced, they felt joy and resolved their minds on bodhicitta, only to later hear this sutra and slander it.

“Kāśyapa! At that time, there will be such signs as these: hearing this sūtra, they will give rise to slander. If there are bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts and uphold the Dharma, they should understand it thus: when [the teaching] accords with the words of the sūtra, they should abandon such persons, because they lack a heart that loves the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time,
those people will themselves proclaim these words:
'I am practicing the bodhisattva path.'"
"Having given rise to madness and dissipation, because of that madness and dissipation, they claim of themselves: 'I am a great Arhat' or 'I am a Pratyekabuddha.
They are incurable, incapable of remaining [in the path], and headed toward the evil realms."
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time there will be no one who performs virtuous deeds, causing many sentient beings to revile bodhi. Kāśyapa!"
At that time, there will be a coarse semblance of form.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time, there will be a person who practices a counterfeit perfection; this shall be the coarse semblance of form in the future age.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time,
those who preach such sūtras as these which speak of reality shall be slandered and reviled, and shall be seen as having abandoned [the truth], their words being called 'teachings of false views.'"
Kāśyapa! At that time, foolish people will not understand that this sutra prohibits the breaking of the precepts. Kāśyapa!

At that time, they will all become evil thieves; not seeing the Dharma for themselves, they will harbor no affliction regarding bodhi, remaining foolishly silent and contemplative, while slandering the non-existence of bodhi.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
at that time there will be no harmonious Saṃgha, though its outward appearance will still exist.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa..."
At that time, many will be ungrateful and will act wickedly with boldness.
What kind of wickedness will they commit?
They will repeatedly utter the name of the Buddha to offer him worship.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at that time, people will revile the precepts of liberation;

they will not guard their verbal karma, and because they do not guard their verbal karma, they will not guard their deportment. Dwelling in impure places, and while dwelling in such impure places, they will expound the Dharma; at that time, my Dharma will gradually become slighted and despised."
The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Threefold Precepts, Scroll One;
The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Threefold Precepts, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
"In this way, gradually many women abandoned their husbands to wander among the monasteries.
Having entered the monasteries, he would preach the Dharma alone for a single woman, teaching her the Dharma of liberation."

Kāśyapa! I see that at that time it will consist entirely of what is not the Dharma: five hundred gates of non-Dharma and five hundred gates of affliction, where no practitioners will cultivate themselves.
At that time, all will be without precepts, no different from householders.
“Kāśyapa! At that time, the dharma of the precepts will be extremely corrupt.

Those who aspire for benefit and seek awakening should not associate with bhikṣuṇīs; they should not dwell in such places, and having distanced themselves from non-association, they must not associate further. They should renounce worldly gain and offerings, relying on the practice of alms-gathering; they should renounce fine clothing and accept rag-robes; they should abandon palaces, towers, couches, and bedding, and instead rely on mountain forests, ravines, and caves as their dwelling; they should renounce all sweet medicinal remedies for illness and rely instead on discarded, stale medicines.”
One should conceive thoughts of affection toward all sentient beings, practice a mind of loving-kindness, and endure all abuse, insults, and physical blows.

Having renounced all acquaintances and kinsmen, one should support oneself through one's own work and not associate with those who remain in the household life; rather, one should follow and practice the precepts of liberation.

“Kāśyapa! If one violates the liberation precepts, one violates the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth; one then violates all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.”

Regarding such retribution for sin: if all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm were to fall into hell, the suffering and pain experienced by those beings would not equal even one hundredth part of this suffering; it would not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even one hundred-thousand-billionth part—it would be beyond the reach of any calculation or analogy.
If one wishes to be free from such sufferings as these, one should abandon such deluded and evil persons by a distance of hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
Even upon merely hearing their voices, one should still keep one's distance; how much more so when seeing or hearing them, yet failing to leave?
One should cultivate one dharma.
What is this one dharma?
That all dharmas are entirely non-existent.
If one endures that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, one should distance oneself from such evil persons and not associate with them.
Furthermore, one should associate with two kinds of dharmas.
What are these two dharmas?
All dharmas are entirely non-existent; yet, while seeking and gathering all dharmas, one does not become attached to the mind that gathers them.
What is meant by "gathering"?

That which has been accumulated is entirely unobtainable; within this unobtainability, one does not give rise to the mind [of grasping]. Just as one abandons wrong views and relinquishes the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), so too should one practice the bodhisattva path in this way—practicing the bodhisattva path while remaining free from all conceptual marks (*nimitta*) and mental activity.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, he renounces all that was described above.
Having renounced these things, he encounters Maitreya Buddha and, freed from all fears, speaks thus:
"How wonderful!"
Peace and happiness!
How wonderful!
To have escaped the company of Māra!
"How wonderful!
I have been distanced from the evil realms.
"Kāśyapa! [the Buddha said.]

If, having heard this sutra, one is neither terrified nor alarmed, and perceives within oneself the arising of a mind capable of upholding it, the Tathāgata knows that such a person is able to uphold my treasury of the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! It is just as when an elder possesses great wealth and rank; the son of that elder regards whatever objects he sees as his father’s property.
When he first sees them, he thinks, "These are my things," and later, carrying these things with him, he stores and keeps them wherever he goes.
"In this way, Kāśyapa! At that time, when a bhikṣu hears such sūtras as these, he thinks to himself:
'This is what has been expounded by the Tathāgata’s soft and wondrous Brahma-voice.'"
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who, having heard this Dharma, gave rise to slander, saying:
"This Dharma-holding bhikṣu speaks thus:
'This is what was spoken by the Buddha; it is the most authentic.'"
"Having few companions, these people will be weak; their dwellings will not be bad, and they will store [their goods] in secret day by day. "Kāśyapa!
In my later age, those who protect the city of the Dharma will be exceedingly few. I entrust these people to Maitreya as their companions, and they shall practice great equanimity (mahopekṣā)."

If there are good sons who, having heard this Dharma, practice according to the teaching, they shall dwell in Maitreya’s first assembly to cultivate the holy life; these beings of right view shall protect the city of the Dharma.

“Kāśyapa! I do not see even a single person who, having failed to encounter me, will—during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish—hear this teaching and not revile it, but instead be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it; such a thing is impossible.”

If they have already seen me and have drawn near to me with reverence, then in the future final age of five hundred years, upon hearing such a sutra as this, they will be able to receive it, uphold it, read it, and recite it.
Such persons as these, without waiting for me to recite this, will naturally possess the mind of omniscience; having thought of me, they will give rise to joy and speak thus:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"The World-Honored One Śākyamuni is able to receive my Dharma and protect me. Therefore, Kāśyapa,
you should train in this Dharma.
"One who studies this Dharma will surely achieve whatever they desire without difficulty.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As I am now, I have forever lost all hope of attaining the unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
If you would cause me to be endowed with all-knowledge, I would be exceedingly joyful.
“If I were to attain the Unsurpassed Way, I would obtain a rare and wondrous physical body.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “I do not praise you;
rather, it is because of you that I speak of these matters, so as to cause those with slight doubts to quickly achieve the unsurpassed, right, and true Way.”

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if there are sentient beings who achieve thirst for the Dharma and achieve its cultivation and fulfillment, these individuals will gradually attain the unsurpassed path; they shall universally sever all veils and entanglements and preach the Dharma for others.
Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva should accomplish four dharmas.
What are these four?
A bodhisattva should arouse great diligence. What is diligence?
Diligence means not seeking form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, but rather accumulating untainted dharmas.
What are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?

They are the absence of the earth element, not speaking of the earth element; the absence of the water, fire, and wind elements, not speaking of the water, fire, and wind elements. All verbal expressions are unreal; this is the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the further shore of verbal expression.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Suppose someone were to ask:”
"The Tathāgata also teaches the Dharma through speech; could it not be unreal?
"World-Honored One!
How should such a person answer?"
"I now wish to hear this from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"In the future, there will be various wicked bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate morality, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom; they will be full of fierce anger and vigorous in their verbal karma, refusing to accept, uphold, read, or recite sūtras such as these."
Why is this? Because these are the teachings expressed in such sūtras as "the arising of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, there will be bhikṣus in the world who give rise to [the notions of] form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, a bhikṣu should dwell in such a manner, just like a householder who never seeks the ultimate truth.
Kāśyapa! It is like a person born blind who wears a golden flower garland, yet does not know it for himself.

Kāśyapa! The bhikṣus of the future will be just like this: even when they hear such sūtras as these, they will be unable to uphold the words, let alone be able to investigate and seek the ultimate truth.

Kāśyapa! It is like a man or a woman who has been rebuked and interrogated by another husband; at a later time, if they hear that husband's name mentioned again, they will be startled, terrified, and filled with dread.

In this way, Kāśyapa, in the final age at the end of time, when the bhikṣus hear this sūtra speak of their actual faults and evils, they will become greedy for robes; recognizing their own transgressions, they will be struck with alarm, fear, and dread.
Kāśyapa! It is just as if a monkey were bound by a yoke and chain, and that monkey’s eyes did not wish to behold such a yoke and chain.
In this same way, Kāśyapa!
Later, the bhikṣus will also be like this: upon hearing such sūtras as these, their eyes will not look upon them with pleasure, and they will turn away and depart. Kāśyapa!
It is just as if a dog were chasing a jackal, and that jackal fled toward a hole in a cemetery or a deep pit.

In this way, Kāśyapa, when bhikṣus of the future hear this sūtra, they will run away like jackals; these jackals will flee because they have violated the prohibitions, and upon hearing such sūtras as these, they will give rise to slander.
Kāśyapa! Just as a jackal runs toward a cemetery, so it is, Kāśyapa!

When future bhikṣus have heard this Dharma, they will rush back to their homes, rush toward sensual desires, rush toward women, rush toward strife, rush toward medical arts, and rush toward legal adjudication; dwelling in these various places, even if they violate the prohibitions and precepts, I say that such people are like those who go to the cemetery.
Kāśyapa! Just as a jackal goes toward a burrow, so it is, Kāśyapa!
At that time, those bhikṣus, with the breakup of the body and the end of life, will go to hell; I say that such as these are "going toward a hole. Kāśyapa!
Just as a jackal runs toward a deep pit, so too will the bhikṣus of the future: with the breakup of the body and the end of life, they will be born in the Spiked Hell.
Kāśyapa! I say that such as these are heading toward a deep pit. Kāśyapa!

Like jackals, these bhikṣus are unable to investigate such sūtras or understand their underlying meaning; they can only engage in such slander and propagate evil, whereby at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they fall into the evil realms.
“Kāśyapa! If there is a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
‘The Dharma you preach is entirely unreal; only the words of the Tathāgata are true.’”
He said to the bhikṣu Abhūtatathatājñāna:
"Venerable sir,
what is it that you currently grasp?"
"Do you grasp at emptiness,
or do you grasp at words? He replied:
"I speak with self-grasping.
He asked: "Are you yourself the Buddha?"
"Why is that? Because you, too, are now relying on verbal expression. He replied:
"I cling to emptiness.
He asked: "This must be analyzed."
Why is this? That which cannot be conceptually differentiated is called emptiness; your "emptiness," however, is merely a verbal expression.
Furthermore, as for your emptiness, is it the emptiness of a self?
"Is it empty because of being empty of a self?
Or is it empty because of being empty of sentient beings? He asked again:
“Bhikṣu! What do you think? Do you delight in the emptiness of all phenomena?”
He replied, "I do not rejoice at all in the emptiness of all phenomena.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir, you have long since lost the Dharma of the Śākya sons of the śramaṇas. Why is this?
For the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that all dharmas are empty; he did not say there is a self, a sentient being, or a life-span, nor did he say there is a person."
He replied: "I now find joy in the emptiness of all phenomena. He asked:
"Venerable sir, you yourself still take delight in the emptiness of all phenomena, let alone the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Venerable sir, what do you think?
Is the eye the Tathāgata?"
“Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the Tathāgata? He replied:
“The eye is the Tathāgata; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the Tathāgata.”
He asked: "This must be distinguished.
If that were so, then you, Great Virtue, would also be a Tathāgata."
He replied: "The eye is a mere verbal designation; it is not the Tathāgata. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are mere verbal designations; they are not the Tathāgata."
He asked: "This must be distinguished.
If the eye is not the Tathāgata, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not the Tathāgata, then how does this accord with what the Great Virtuous One previously stated?"
"If the Tathāgata is indeed speech, why do you now say that he is not? He replied:
"The eye is not the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata is not apart from the eye."
"Even the mind is not the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata is not apart from the mind.
He asked: "The Tathāgata has said that the twelve bases (āyatana) are sentient beings; this should be analyzed."
"Venerable Sir!
Are the eye and forms the Tathāgata?
And so on, up to: are the mind and mental phenomena the Tathāgata?"
He replied: "The eye and forms are the Tathāgata; even so, the mind and mental phenomena are the Tathāgata. He asked:
"As you have said, all sentient beings are the Tathāgata; all lands, all mountains, forests, trees, grasses, and shrubs are entirely the Tathāgata."
He replied: "The eye is not the Tathāgata, and so on, up to: the mind is not the Tathāgata. He asked:
"If that is so, then do you say that the Tathāgata is the Dharma or not the Dharma?
He replied, "Form is not the Tathāgata, and so on, up to: phenomena are not the Tathāgata."
He asked: "Venerable Sir!
Is the Dharma not the Tathāgata?"
He replied, "The Dharma is not the Tathāgata. He asked:

"If that were so, there are sentient beings who say there are no parents, no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, and no impure lineages; they commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, greed, anger, and wrong views—would all such people, according to what you have said, be Tathāgatas?"
He replied: "That which is not unwholesome is called the Tathāgata. He asked:
"If that were so, as you have said, the Dharma is not the Tathāgata, and what is not the Dharma is not the Tathāgata.
If it is neither the Dharma nor non-Dharma, then there is no verbal expression."
"As the Venerable One has said, that which is beyond verbal expression is called the Tathāgata. "Kāśyapa!
You should repeatedly subdue such wicked people in this manner."

Kāśyapa! Among the people, devas, māras, and brahmās in the world, I see none who can engage in discourse with one who speaks thus in accordance with the Dharma, except for those who are intolerant due to hatred and delusion, or those who, lacking any valid reason, revile the teaching of emptiness and depart.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you all should uphold such a sūtra as this. Kāśyapa!
In future ages, there will be those who uphold this Dharma, and they shall have three names.
What are these three? They are:
one who speaks of annihilation, one who speaks of non-existence, and one who speaks of the absence of an aggregate of aggregates, lacking in reverence.
Kāśyapa! At that time, sūtras such as these will be subjected to slander. Kāśyapa!
Observe this moment: you did not revere the Buddha, you did not revere the Dharma, and you did not revere the Saṅgha.
If one does not revere the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, what kind of monk can be said to dwell [in the community]?
They rely merely on verbal expressions and depend solely on names.
Although they chant the Buddha’s name and proclaim it among the assembly, they cannot see what the Buddha actually is.
Although they preach the Dharma with their mouths, they do not know how the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, preaches the Dharma.
Although they speak these words:

"The four paths and the four fruits constitute the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas of the Buddha, the World-Honored One," they know only the names, yet they do not understand the actual virtues that correspond to those names; for the sake of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, they slander the Dharma.

A bodhisattva should apply diligent effort toward this; regarding such sūtras as these, they should give rise to a rare longing and joy, and should receive, uphold, read, and recite them. Why is this?
This person shall protect the city of the Dharma in future lives. Why is this?
Because for ninety-one kalpas they have not heard the exposition of this teaching on emptiness.

“Kāśyapa! I now reflect upon a past eon of a thousand kalpas; at that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śānti (Quiescence), whose lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, who protected bodhisattvas and benefited the world.”
Furthermore, there was a Tathāgata named Vigataraja, whose lifespan was twenty-one kalpas; he practiced the bodhisattva path for that duration before finally attaining the unsurpassed way. Kāśyapa!
Observe, Kāśyapa, how many difficult practices the Tathāgata performs to gather in all sentient beings!
At the end of the kalpa-turbidity, one should not revile this.
Why is this? Kāśyapa! When the kalpa-turbidity has reached its end, it is extremely rare for there to be even a single person who can believe in this Dharma.
At that time, those who uphold this Dharma will not be harmed by swords, staves, tiles, or stones;
this is truly rare.
Why is this so, Kāśyapa?

This Dharma is the Dharma of the Great Mahāsattvas; it is the teaching that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-conditioned. It cannot be understood by those who are attached to the view of a self (*ātman*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva*), the view of a life-force (*jīva*), the view of a person (*pudgala*), or the view of existence (*bhava*).

Furthermore, it concerns those who rely on views—namely, reliance on the view of precepts, the view of a Buddha, the view of the Dharma, the view of the Saṅgha, or the view of Nirvāṇa. If anyone gives rise to a view of Nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata knows that this is entirely a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Why is this? Kāśyapa! The Tathāgata does not possess nirvāṇa, nor does he attain nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa! If there were such a thing as nirvāṇa or one who attains nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata would declare that all such views are false views;
and if one holds false views, they are said to be devoid of wisdom.
Those who are harmed by a lack of wisdom are foolish worldlings.
If it is difficult even for foolish worldlings to be born in heaven, how much more so is it to attain the Bodhi of a Buddha? "Kāśyapa!..."

In future ages there will be bhikṣus who are twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, or even a hundred years old—aged and senile, lacking wisdom—who, though adorned with robes and having shaved their hair and altered their appearance, are foolish and decrepit men devoid of majestic virtue who give rise to perverse deeds.
At the time of death, they further commit evil deeds and disparage the Dharma of the precepts.
By means of these three matters, they practice deceit and fraud.
What are the three?
To manifest dignified deportment, to manifest the practice of ethical discipline, and the marks of a virtuous person;
to raise a finger as a sign, using such methods to display one's own virtues—this constitutes falling into great arrogance.
Dying with a mind of delusion and regret, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life,
one falls into hell. Therefore, Kāśyapa, I now proclaim:
"I am your true spiritual friend; I instruct you, desiring to benefit you and out of compassion for you, so that you will not suffer great torment in the future."

"Kāśyapa! I never permit one who clings to the view of sentient beings to go forth; nor do I truly permit one who clings to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, or the view of a person to go forth."
If one merely asserts my Dharma and then leaves the household life, consuming the heavy offerings of the faithful, yet lacks the true merit of upholding the precepts— Kāśyapa!

It would be better for a person to abstain from food and drink for six days than to accept the offerings of the faithful while clinging to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, and even the view of nirvāṇa.
"A bodhisattva should apply diligent effort within this [teaching], remaining unattached to anything from the view of a self up to the view of nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa, I entrust such sūtras as these to such virtuous men."
Why is this? Because the practices of these individuals are identical to my own practice.
Such persons are my comrades; they are my companions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings beset by suffering and affliction Have none at all to provide rescue or protection,
Except for the Teacher of the World, The one who is free from conceptual proliferation."
Sentient beings afflicted by various sufferings, who rely upon inferior paths, gradually increase their various desires; because of this, they fall into the evil realms.
Without a guide and without benefit, they dwell in places that are perilous and desolate.
Those who follow an improper path will never find peace and security.
It is like one carrying wealth and treasures who travels through a wilderness seeking profit;
when a band of thieves arises, everything is plundered.
Having lost their wealth, they return home; having failed to gain profit, their suffering increases.
Borrowing wealth from others, their misery thereby doubles;
these people are just like this—having created karma, they have not yet repaid it.
The white karma one has created oneself returns to consume this very wealth.
Those who rely on robbery, those ordinary persons fallen into wrong views,
cling to the view of a self, the view of a life-principle, and the view of a person.
Those bhikṣus who preach the Dharma of emptiness, yet rely on views of a self and a person,
will give rise to a mind of slander and swiftly fall into the evil realms.
They will give rise to and cultivate hatred, further disparaging and reviling one another.
Those who slander and speak what is untrue, yet feel shame and remorse for this;
those whose bodily and verbal actions are evil, whose mental karma is utterly deceitful and sycophantic,
and who stubbornly cling to various views— they go to the most wretched realms.
Having committed evil deeds, one swiftly arrives at an evil destination,
where one undergoes manifold sufferings and afflictions, with no one to provide protection or refuge.
In future ages, there will be those whose anger is fierce and intense.
Those who lack compassion will revile such sūtras as these, which urge on those bhikṣus pressed by the intensity of suffering toward awakening;
they will fail to give rise to faith and reverence for the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas.
They give rise to mutual disputes and quickly incite great anger and contention;
they slander and defame one another, spreading their evil throughout all directions.
They create various kinds of calumny, heaping it upon those who possess a sense of shame.
When evil friends gain power and those who are gentle are weak and inferior,
when one knows the True Dharma has become feeble and unwholesome dharmas increase in strength—
then this bhikṣu should depart, for he is my beloved son.
To what place should one go to find a state of peace and security?
There, those who commit many evils are released, for they have no compassion here.
Such sūtras as these, I shall always keep in mind.
The Teacher has spoken thus; by this I find delight.
I shall go to that place praised by the Buddha, for in this time when the Dharma is decaying, those who are gentle are hard to find.
Some spoke these words:
"One should quickly leave this place and go to the Great Sage, the place where the unsurpassed path is attained.
Others spoke these words:
“Excellent! These words are well spoken.
The Guide has said thus:
‘One should travel to pay homage at the various stūpas.’”
One should rather go to this place, the delightful Bodhi tree,
than to that place of envy, hatred, anger, and strife.
That bhikṣu then departed, practicing as I have taught.
Seeing these other dwelling places— those said to be where the Buddha dwelt,
his places for walking meditation and sitting, whether on stone or in open spaces—
they flocked to those sites and wept repeatedly as they gazed upon one another.
"This is the abode of the Great Seer, the place where he practiced walking meditation and enjoyed his stay;
it was here that the Buddha originally dwelt, yet though one sees this place, the Buddha is not seen.
This unsurpassed Seer has taught the unsurpassed Dharma."
We do not see them now; all conditioned things are impermanent.
Humans and non-humans alike, as well as devas and nāgas, have all come together;
they were gladdened by his excellent teaching, yet we do not see them now.
Arriving at this dwelling place— namely, beneath the Bodhi tree—
and having gathered here, they practiced right mindfulness and wise reflection.
At that time, the World’s Teacher attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
The hosts of Māra are struck with terror, like small jackals;
this is the site of the original path of practice, the place where the Tathāgata sat.
All Buddhas of the past and future have likewise sat upon this very seat.
This is the valiant one, revered by billions of devas;
sitting cross-legged for seven days, he gazes upon this king of trees.
Having made this offering, the man proceeds once more to the place where the Dharma is taught.
At this place the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and its sound reached the Brahma world.
A bhikṣu went there and wept again and again, saying:
"The Valiant One has come here; he has tamed these five men."
When the five men saw the Buddha, they immediately gave rise to distress and anxiety;
together they deliberated on evil, resolving that none of them should rise [to greet him].
Yet this World-Honored One of Great Compassion, having aroused a heart of pity for the multitude, [approached them].
He preached for the five bhikṣus, turning the nectar-like words of the Dharma.
Having paid homage at the site of the Turning of the Wheel, he wept again and again;
proceeding further to the site of Nirvāṇa, he beheld the Buddha’s final resting place.
At that time, the World’s Guide, who benefits many sentient beings, shattered and broke his own body; thus did the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa. Alas!
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Śākya Lion, the Muni—now I hear only his name, yet do not behold his form.
This unsurpassed Seer, Suvīra, was the very last;
having known this through great wisdom, he realized: "This is my final birth."
Whether they pass away while traveling, or pass away while staying in one place,
or pass away at the conclusion of their travels, they shall all be reborn in auspicious realms.
In the future age of the final dharma, this vast Buddha-dharma—
Such a person shall attain nirvāṇa.
Yet if a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts receives universal offerings and,
having consumed these heavy provisions, quickly departs for the evil realms.
Observe these bhikṣus, who possess such varying degrees of excellence;
the wise, at the end of their lives, will swiftly attain rebirth in heaven.
These are the lamps that illuminate the world, those who have compassion for the world.
The Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom, with a compassionate heart benefiting sentient beings,
dwells among those engaged in worldly affairs with a mind of leaping joy and delight,
thinking: "I shall surely attain Buddhahood, and I shall also meet Maitreya."
When making offerings to that Blessed One before the entire assembly, the Omniscient One prophesied of me:
"Just as I have intended, you shall possess great power. Thus I have spoken this meaning.
Although they do not see the Buddha, one should know that it is as if facing him directly.
I shall comfort them, and likewise I shall practice the factors of enlightenment and pay homage to all Buddhas.
If there are women who turn toward unsurpassed bodhi,
I shall likewise comfort them, as will immeasurable Tathāgatas.
Having cast off this female body, they shall quickly attain a male body.
Having seen Maitreya, one should make offerings to him.
Whatever one seeks shall all be fulfilled according to one's wishes;
by following and learning from this wise one, one will give rise to a profound and firm aspiration.
Having developed firm desire, one who maintains the precepts and possesses extensive learning shall receive a prophecy from Maitreya Buddha.
Therefore, hearing these benefits, give rise to noble and virtuous faith.
With firm faith one proceeds toward it, gathering in all sentient beings.
Who could seek this state and fail to attain it?
For those with wisdom and diligence, awakening is not difficult to obtain.
Without a mind of flattery or crookedness, practicing and cultivating a compassionate mind,
always dwelling in a secluded and tranquil place— this is called the practice of bodhi.
Abandoning such places, one speaks only of the place of bodhi.
This is a great thief of greed, from which all should distance themselves.
If, for the sake of food and drink, as well as matters of profit and gain,
one falsely pretends to uphold the True Dharma and mutually proclaims it to others.
This is an impure way of life; living by means of delusion, one is harmed by manifold evils and beset by the lower realms.
This is but a single-flavored Dharma-gate, yet they merely bear the name of "bhikṣu."
Those who slander such a Dharma, as well as the precepts of liberation—
if there are those who uphold the precepts and I have taught the laws of restraint,
yet they, like counterfeit bhikṣus, should slander them— they shall not reach the state of the noble ones.
The entire world of gods and humans will all abandon and depart from them;
even the World-Honored One of All-Knowledge will doubly distance himself from such a person.
If one has no evil karma of body, nor any evil karma of speech, [one shall not suffer such a fate].
With mental karma entirely purified, they swiftly attain nirvana.

"Kāśyapa! After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final age of the latter dharma, there will be bhikṣus who have planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas and who will all enter parinirvāṇa; those of purely virtuous life-span will pass away until none remain."

In the final five hundred years, there will be bhikṣus who are insatiable in their greed, full of anger and divisiveness, coarse, harsh, and malicious; with angry faces and knitted brows, they will abide in these three dharmas.
What are these three? They are:
devoting oneself exclusively to the practice of medicine, dwelling in the business of trade, and associating with women.
Abiding in these three dharmas, one shall lose four dharmas.
What are the four? They are:
the loss of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the loss of the wholesome path, the loss of the attainment of fruition, and the loss of the vision of phenomena as they truly are.
Once a person has incurred these four things, they further cause four other things to blaze up intensely.
What are these four dharmas? They are:

the intense burning of envy, the intense burning of malice, the intense burning of coveting other families, and the intense burning of attachment to the accumulation of gains and offerings; they take as their occupation the greedy love for clothing and the making of chests and baskets—being thus empty and possessing nothing, they lack the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Having heard this Dharma, one will fall into four states.
What are these four?
One falls into slandering the Dharma; one speaks at inappropriate times; one preaches the Dharma exclusively for women; and one gradually violates the precepts.
"Having heard such teachings as these, they fall into calamity. Kāśyapa,
it is just like a vicious dog that strikes its own nose."
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Would this dog not be even more wicked?
He replied, “It is so;
it shall increase evil manifold.
The Buddha said:

“Kāśyapa! These wicked people are like those evil dogs or like piśācas. If a bhikṣu of pure intent upholds such teachings and speaks such teachings, being truly of few desires and praising the state of having few desires;”

Having heard this, they will be struck with wonder and disbelief; they will sink into cowardice and weakness, give rise to affliction and feverish distress, and further increase their anger—what kind of karma will they dwell within?
This time has not yet arrived, yet I now speak of it in advance.
Upon hearing this sutra, they will give rise to slander; as if pierced by a spear, they will become greatly enraged and say:
"This was not spoken by the Buddha."
Those who disparage those with few desires speak thus:
"One should call this person one of many desires; he is not one of few desires. Kāśyapa!

I have always praised in various ways those who have few desires, those who are content, those who observe the *poṣadha* well, those who are easy to dwell with, those who practice the *dhūta* austerities, those who dwell in forest hermitages, and those who maintain a pure livelihood. You should not associate with such people of mixed and evil conduct, nor be their equals.
Why is this? This is the dharma of householders; do not use such dharmas to deceive others.
This is the dharma of householders; you should not give rise to great anger or resentment.
"You should not amass great quantities of wealth; you must relinquish riches and treasures.
You must take care never to manifest extraordinary signs or to praise your own virtues.
You should remain free from attachment and not store up possessions in excess."
"You should not keep camels, horses, oxen, or donkeys;
you should not be indolent or lazy, but should instead be diligent and energetic, abandoning unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas."
“Kāśyapa! I have always, through various causes and conditions, praised the forest hermitage as pure and tranquil, and as being far removed from intimacy with households.
Yet in the future final age, people will contravene this teaching of mine; having contravened my Dharma, they will seek to create manifold afflictions and slander the True Dharma.”
Kāśyapa! It is just as if there were a person who, while suffering from heat, drank ghee; having drunk it, he became afflicted with thirst and said to another person, "Give me water."
The man replied: "Excellent, Great Being!
Do not seek water; because you have consumed ghee, do not let this cause your death."
That person, filled with anger and resentment, reviles and insults this other person; because he does not comply with him, he drinks [the poison] and dies at the end of his life.
In this same way, Kāśyapa, in the future there will be bhikṣus who are attached to views and abide in various evils, and they will address another bhikṣu in this manner:
Thinking, "This matter should be adhered to;
this should not be adhered to," they instead give rise to anger, slandering and reviling, and denouncing such sūtras as well as the Tathāgata’s teachings.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, such persons as these contend and compete against the Tathāgata. Kāśyapa!

"Observe this bhikṣu Bhadrapāla: when he heard that the Tathāgata had established the precepts so that the community of bhikṣus should eat while seated in a single session, he became enraged and did not come to my presence for three months."

Kāśyapa! At that time, those whose pure conduct was complete and perfect were still able to act in such a manner; how much more so after my parinirvāṇa, when people are attached to food and drink, attached to robes, bowls, bedding, and medicinal requisites, overwhelmed by sleep, and filled with intense anger?
Having heard such sūtras as these, they do not even show respect to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, let alone toward other bhikṣus who practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Kāśyapa! If such teachings as these were to disappear and be extinguished, it would be most unwholesome; it would be exceedingly unwholesome.

“Kāśyapa! If a son of good family desires to seek wholesome benefit and has faith in this Dharma of mine, then during the final age of the dharma-ending period—a time of turbid evil, calamities, and transformations; at the end of my teaching, an age of dregs and impurity; when anger is rampant and virtuous people are difficult to find—[he should uphold it].”
At that time, if there are those who hear and believe such profound sutras, one should believe that these people are practicing in accordance with the truth and not otherwise;
one should say they accept them with faith and not that they do not accept them.
Kāśyapa! I now also speak that which is called "correspondence," not non-correspondence, and not lack of faith. Kāśyapa!

It is just as when a vicious horse is yoked together with a well-trained horse; if it cannot remain calm and quiet without even being tamed, how much less could it endure the blowing of conchs, the striking of bells, or the beating of drums? Such a thing is impossible.
In this way, Kāśyapa,
it is impossible for a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts to be able to endure the dharmas of a true man. Kāśyapa!
Just as a wicked horse is startled and terrified by a single stroke of the whip, so it is, Kāśyapa:

if those who are attached to the notion of a self hear even a single teaching on non-self and emptiness, they become startled, terrified, and fearful, giving rise to contention; how much more so when it is taught extensively!
