“Kāśyapa! You should arouse the faculty of great diligence and don the great armor, subduing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Māras, so that they shall never again give rise to contention.”

How does one arouse the faculty of diligence? Freedom from desire is the faculty of diligence; the merits of *dhūta* practices are the faculty of diligence; freedom from greed is the faculty of diligence; freedom from delusion and freedom from hatred are the faculty of diligence; freedom from envy is the faculty of diligence; renunciation of desire is the faculty of diligence; being solitary and without companion is the faculty of diligence; freedom from sloth and torpor is the faculty of diligence; at all times not giving rise to any evil thoughts is the faculty of diligence; at all times not giving rise to thoughts of desire is the faculty of diligence;
not giving rise to doubt, but arousing great diligence and remaining free from all doubt—this is the faculty of diligence.

Having abandoned all doubt and completed the great adornments, one resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) without any dependence; how much less, then, should one give rise to the notion of a self?

One should never give rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-force, the notion of a person, the notion of male, or the notion of female. One should not give rise to the notions of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element; one should not give rise to the notions of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; one should not give rise to the notion of precepts or the notion of violating precepts; one should not give rise to the notion of emptiness. Indeed, one should not give rise to any notions whatsoever, even the notion of nirvana should not be given rise to.
"What is meant by 'not giving rise to any perceptions'?
Can such perceptions be found therein? Kāśyapa!"
If desire is unreal, then one who knows the extinction of desire is likewise unreal.
Kāśyapa! Desire has no fixed location; it is merely a false discourse. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks according to reality.
"This desire is not my dharma; it is a dharma of cessation. What is the dharma of cessation?

If one clings to non-attachment, that clinging itself becomes a conception as vast as Mount Sumeru. If a person harbors such a conception, know that this person has ruined and lost the noble Dharma; they cannot give rise to the qualities of a śramaṇa and do not abide in the qualities of a śramaṇa. Such a person is called a fool, a deluded one, who can never give rise to the qualities of a śramaṇa."
Why is this? Because those who harbor such attachments have been held in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas. “Kāśyapa!
It is like observing the bhikṣu Kokālika, the bhikṣu Devadatta, the bhikṣu Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, the bhikṣu Kālaka, and the bhikṣu Sāgara.

Kāśyapa! The bhikṣu Aśvajit, the bhikṣu Pūrṇa, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra were my personal attendants; they heard me speak directly from my presence, saw me walking in meditation, saw me sitting upright, and saw me manifesting supernatural powers by walking through the air, as well as my subduing of hundreds of thousands of non-Buddhists. Yet even such individuals as these did not give rise to a wholesome mind toward me; because of the insects beneath their feet that acted in opposition to me, they brought themselves to the evil realms.

If one were to speak truthfully of the Tathāgata’s merits, one should take sandalwood powder as vast as Mount Sumeru and scatter it upon him to form a great precious canopy as large as the triple-thousandfold world system, while standing in the void above that person.
Why is this? Kāśyapa!

Those who possess the mind of faith and invoke the name of the Buddha are few indeed; how much rarer are those who, having already given rise to faith, leave the household life to follow the Buddha, distancing themselves from the defilements of desire and cultivating non-attached dhyāna—this is truly most rare.
“Kāśyapa! If sentient beings are able to uphold the prohibitive precepts I have taught and believe and understand such ambrosial Dharma, it is all the more rare and extraordinary. Kāśyapa!”
It is like a great multitude gathering at a shrine to fashion a leather chest, its form exquisitely crafted and painted with various colors, yet filled with filth and excrement.
If someone were to wrap it in fine upper garments, carry it about, and show it to others, those among them who perceive its unreality would turn their backs and abandon it.
In this way, Kāśyapa,
if there is a bhikṣu who beholds the sacrificial altar of the Tathāgata’s qualities of dharma, yet within that assembly there is a bhikṣu who harbors the notion of a self, Kāśyapa!
If there is the notion of self, desire arises; if there is the notion of another, desire arises.
Kāśyapa, one who is without the notion of self will not give rise to anger upon hearing such sūtras as these.
Why is this? To disparage others is unwholesome; for this reason, having heard this Dharma, one attains a virtuous mind.
If there is attachment to the mark of a self, this constitutes a false view.
If those with wrong views hear such true instructions as these, they will give rise to anger.
Why is this? Kāśyapa!
Those who possess the notion of a self give rise to anger. Kāśyapa!

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, upon hearing such teachings as these, should give rise to anger and slander them, such people merely possess the outward form and name of a śramaṇa; I am not their teacher, and they are not my disciples.
Why is this? One who speaks falsely is not my disciple, and I am not the teacher of one who speaks falsely. Why is this?
Kāśyapa! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is a speaker of truth; the Tathāgata declares that all phenomena are empty. Kāśyapa!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has destroyed all notions of self; therefore, such a person contends with the Tathāgata. Whoever contends with the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is said to be Māra. The Tathāgata does not permit those who belong to the faction of Māra to leave the household life or receive full ordination.
Kāśyapa! If one were to say that a small horse is born from a nāga-elephant, Kāśyapa!
"What do you think?
Is the speech of such a person to be trusted? Kāśyapa replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
"Kāśyapa, is this statement consistent with reason?"
"No, World-Honored One! Kāśyapa,

At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “How marvelous, World-Honored One!

What are the four?

relying on their own physical vigor, relying on their own strength, being stained by and attached to the five desires while indulging in and craving alcohol, and failing to give rise to wholesome thoughts.

Kāśyapa! In this way, Kāśyapa, those who grasp at all phenomena,

In this way, they cling to the notions of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and cling to the signs of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they perform what is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa and not the Dharma of a brāhmaṇa. They cling to the notions of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and cling to the signs of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; they perform what is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa and not the Dharma of a brāhmaṇa.
They cling to pure observance of the precepts and cling to the marks of observing the precepts as they seek awakening.
They cling to extensive learning and cling to the marks of extensive learning as they seek awakening.
To be attached to shame and remorse, or attached to coming and going, is to practice what is not the dharma of a śramaṇa and not the dharma of a brāhmaṇa.
If one is attached, one will be harmed by it.
What is meant by "being harmed"?
One is harmed by greed, harmed by hatred, and harmed by delusion.
To be attached to the perception of the eye is to be attached to the characteristics of the eye; one is thus harmed by the eye through attachment to forms that are either pleasing or unpleasing.
In this way, one clings to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; because of this clinging, one is harmed by the mind—that is, by agreeable and disagreeable phenomena.
If one is harmed, then one is deceived.

Those who are harmed—namely those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, as well as humans and devas—all suffer such harm because of their attachments. It is due to these attachments that they are harmed by them.
In this context, what is meant by "conceiving of notions"?

It refers to conceiving of the notion of a self, conceiving of the notion of "mine," conceiving of the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and conceiving of the notions of a skeleton, of decay, of blueness, of worms, of being smeared with blood, of fragility, and of liberation. Yet, regarding this liberation, what notion could there possibly be that one would still cling to?

That is to say, they cling to the notion that liberation shall be attained here; they cling to the immeasurable places of birth in the past, clinging to the thought, "I shall remember those places"; they cling to the future and to the present, giving rise to such conceptions as:
"I am the past" and "I am the present."
"Wherever they may be, they give rise to conceptual attachments, even toward nirvāṇa.
They form this thought, saying:
'I shall attain nirvāṇa.'"
"Arising from such conceptions, Kāśyapa!
To speak briefly, everything up to and including whatever mental conceptions one may have is called 'attachment'; even the conception of emptiness is called 'the conception of attachment'."

All such things are neither the dharma of śramaṇas nor the dharma of brāhmaṇas; they are neither the practice of śramaṇas nor the practice of brāhmaṇas—such is the dharma of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as taught by the Tathāgata.
“Kāśyapa! It is just as space and the great earth do not form such thoughts:

you shall quickly attain it, just as I have quickly attained it.

though you claim to be arhats, in truth you possess overweening pride.

They slander the Bodhi, which belongs to the Dharma King;
the devas are filled with extreme sorrow and pain, weeping again and again until they faint and fall to the ground.

Since you have heard the Buddha-dharma yourself, you shall not hear it again;
yet this Buddha, throughout incalculable eons, has endured for both himself and others—
when will such a sentient being attain Buddhahood?

has now proclaimed the True Dharma, which shall now perish and be forever exhausted.
Now that the ruin of the Dharma arises, the most extreme violence and evil are being committed.
The messengers of Māra are most evil; those with few desires are weak and inferior.
Deceitful and lacking wisdom, these illusory and false petty worldlings give rise to fierce anger and slander the Dharma of the Sugata.
Having heard the voice of the Earth-God, the gods of the heavens were struck with wonder;
the Four Great Kings and their peers, having heard it, were filled with sorrow and distress.

All shared in sorrowful tears, raising loud cries and lamentations.

all the devas gathered there and spoke to one another about what was on their minds:
All the adorned cities, composed of various jewels, lack all luster and color,
appearing like mere heaps of earth; these cities possess no majesty or virtue,

This city lacks majesty and splendor; it is as lovely and delightful as it was before.

having seen it, they fell to the ground in a swoon—such shall be their retribution.

Down to Jambudvīpa, One beholds the sight of great destruction.

For seven days, the Victorious One lacked his majestic radiance;
for those seven days, the gods wept again and again:

Having come to the city of Śrāvastī to pay our respects,"

the world is no longer a place of joy.

when the kings of Jambudvīpa destroy the Buddha’s stūpas and monasteries,

and there are certain bhikṣuṇīs who likewise fall into the evil realms.
There are those who break the precepts while living at home, as well as lay upāsakas who dwell in the household.
Having uttered such a great and evil cry, they shall surely go to the evil realms.
There are certain wicked women who likewise go to those most evil places;
at that time, when such things occur, the entire world will tremble.
Some flee to the villages; some run to the mountains and forests.
All sentient beings are driven in haste, and few remain alive.
There will be many bandits and thieves, as well as widespread famines.
The five grains were sown but did not ripen; locusts wrought havoc and disaster.
At that time, grain and rice became exceedingly expensive, and among those whose lives came to an end, they fell after death into the realm of hungry ghosts, where they underwent manifold sufferings.
In all places where there are stūpas and monasteries, for the Saṃgha of the four quarters,
at that time the bhikṣus shall divide and take them among themselves.
Such manifold sufferings as these [shall arise] after my parinirvāṇa.
One should act with swift diligence; do not wait for such a time.
Ordinary people lack wisdom, and ordinary people lack insight;
having performed the deeds of ordinary people, they swiftly fall into the evil realms.
One should diligently recite and chant; from the source of wisdom, one should teach sentient beings with wisdom so that they may swiftly reach the auspicious paths.
Illuminating with the light of wisdom, one should train as I have.
Abandoning all afflictions, one swiftly reaches nirvāṇa.
Since the True Dharma will not long remain, you should be firm and diligent in your vigor;
thus do I exhort you: you should practice correctly.
In the time after my parinirvāṇa, during the sixty intermediate kalpas,
who would not feel love upon hearing the name of the Buddha?
Driven by the torment of hunger, they shall gather together from all sides.
They eat the flesh of their mothers and children, doing so to one another in turn.
When any infant is born, they do not allow it to go to other houses;
though the child remains at ease within its own room, it still feels great terror.
Those who have seen or heard this—such is the suffering of birth and death.
Who would give rise to craving?
It arises from the root of a lack of wisdom; the origin of desire is the woman.
It gives rise to the roots of all suffering; therefore, one should abandon suffering.
If there are deluded sentient beings who associate with lustful women, while those who possess wisdom swiftly reach nirvana.
The suffering produced by unwholesome karma manifests as its retribution;
this fruit is with outflows (*sāsrava*), and for this reason one falls into the evil realms.
If all phenomena are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are empty and non-existent.
"One who is not firm and lacks tranquility should swiftly practice the Path.
Kāśyapa! This is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished the first dharma."
If one has a mind that desires and delights in untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), one should not abide in any dharmas while teaching all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
A bodhisattva should act with firmness and abide with firmness.
What is acting with firmness?
What is abiding with firmness?
One should firm up the mind and one should firm up diligence.
In this context, what is called "firming the mind" and what is called "firming diligence"?

Kāśyapa! One of firm resolve, a bodhisattva should give rise to such a mind as this: only after making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River does he then give rise to a single thought-moment.

If not even a single Buddha were to appear throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and if one were to again give rise to such thoughts as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, thereby obtaining a human body, and obtaining bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, hearing a single phrase of the Dharma and increasing this wisdom until it reaches the Unsurpassed Way—
this is the kind of mind that a bodhisattva generates.
This bodhisattva reflects:
"I should now practice such difficult and arduous austerities, diligently and vigorously cultivating the wisdom of the Buddha; I should now seek it in this manner."
“Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva should maintain such firm resolve. Kāśyapa!”
I cite this analogy so that those who possess wisdom may understand through metaphor!

Kāśyapa, if awakening were attained through such ascetic practices, one would not be indolent for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; rather, one would study diligently without slackening, studying tirelessly for eons equal to the sands of the Ganges to attain awakening.
The Bodhisattva thought:
"I should now generate firm resolve and firm desire; I shall never abandon the unsurpassed right path. Kāśyapa!
A bodhisattva should thus firm his mind. Kāśyapa!
If there is a bodhisattva who firms his mind in this way, what is it that he takes up?
This means not grasping at what is possible (*sthāna*) and not grasping at what is impossible (*asthāna*).
How does one not grasp at what is possible and what is impossible?
If both the possible and the impossible are entirely non-existent, they do not obstruct *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and it is swiftly accomplished.

Kāśyapa! Suppose one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift; yet, if another person were to seek out, investigate, rely upon, and abide by such sūtras as those now expounded by the Tathāgata—the very place where the true eye of bodhi is directed—this latter person’s mass of merit would be many times greater and more excellent than that.
Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva should maintain such firm resolve, yet must not grasp at this firm resolve, nor cease from it.
How does one who is a beginner cultivate the roots of merit of a beginner?
What is meant by "planting many"?
It does not mean that a single mind can know many karmas. Why is this?
Because this Dharma cannot be expressed in words, one should constantly perform many kinds of preliminary practices within it, namely, firm resolve.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The mind does not create the marks of the mind; There is always great terror therein.”
"Shall I attain it or not? What shall become of this matter?
Thus one constantly gives rise to doubting thoughts regarding everything.
While dwelling in these states, one practices the means of cultivation; how then can one attain bodhi?
That is the notion of indolence, not the notion of bodhi;
therein lies all doubt regarding both the Buddha and the śrāvakas.
Longing for it but failing to reach it, they do not attain the excellent dharmas of the Buddhas.
It is not by means of sounds that one can attain peace and happiness.
One who possesses faith and desire for the Dharma can accumulate the most supreme excellence;
it is not through mere minor reflection that one can obtain the sublime path.
"Among all dharmas, one should abide in a single dharma;
once awakened wisdom has increased, one practices to attain the Way. Kāśyapa!"
When this Dharma was being taught, if there were a bodhisattva who had accomplished this practice but had not encountered a Buddha, and yet spoke of himself, saying:
"I shall become a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Kāśyapa! A lay bodhisattva should act in this way. How, then, should they practice to attain bodhi? Kāśyapa!"
A lay bodhisattva has three kinds of action for seeking awakening.
What are the three? They are:
generating an intense aspiration, not being attached to original actions regarding omniscience, and upholding the five precepts.
Possessing these three parts, one proceeds toward six dharmas. What are the six? One attains the noble Dharma;

one’s faculties are complete, being neither blind, nor deaf, nor mute; one does not have an ugly appearance; one quickly gains faith; one does not fear the profound Dharma; and having heard it, one quickly understands and swiftly attains non-retrogression. One should be fully endowed with these six dharmas.
One should thoroughly understand the five obstructing dharmas.
What are these five?

One should recognize double-tongued speech and never speak falsely; a bodhisattva should perceive stinginess as an obstruction to the bodhisattva path and therefore remain unstingy; and if one is attached to sensual desires, this is an obstruction to the bodhisattva path, so one must never indulge in such desires.
These five dharmas can create obstacles.
Furthermore, one should also practice three dharmas.
What are these three?

One should constantly maintain the aspiration to leave the household life; one should reverently and respectfully receive instruction from śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who purely uphold the precepts, while always remaining far removed from those who preach the Dharma by clinging to signs of existence.
Why is this? Because these are not things that a bodhisattva should study.
A bodhisattva should not carry false grass.
Why is this? Because it is not bodhi. If one carries what is unreal, this constitutes an obstacle to learning; one does not learn the dharma of accumulation.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should train in three dharmas.
What are these three?
With a mind constantly focused on the goal of attaining Buddhahood, one should diligently practice recitation and study, and always cultivate a heart of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
One should thus cultivate and assemble these three dharmas.
Furthermore, one should cultivate three dharmas. What are these three?
To abstain from beating and striking others; not to speak of others as being lowly or base; and to act as a savior for sentient beings who are afraid.
"One should draw near to these three kinds of persons.
He then spoke in verse:
"Do not associate with inferior people; Do not look upon those who are not upright."
Having seen them, one should keep far away, as one would distance oneself from a venomous snake.
One should not train under them, nor should one pay them homage;
one should avoid them utterly, as if seeing a vicious dog.
Such a person falls into the evil realms; those who possess attachment to signs, even if they practice this study, will likewise go that way.
Having heard the Buddha-dharma, one should have no doubt regarding the dharma of emptiness.
And those bhikṣus who delight in emptiness—toward them this reverence is born.
In this state, their learning increases, and sharp wisdom is likewise produced;
they draw near to the path of enlightenment and become objects of veneration for all.
Swiftly receive the precepts of the fast; having swiftly received them, recite them.
This increases wisdom, like a blue lotus in water.
Swiftly receive the precepts of the fast, and listen extensively to the Dharma.
This increases wisdom, thereby severing all outflows and fetters.
With great wisdom and great diligence, possessing great majesty and fearlessness,
one performs benefit for oneself and brings advantage to others.
He never strikes others; he should delight in such [conduct], advancing in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). For such a person, the Dharma does not diminish.
Such a person has few ailments and possesses the most supreme and wondrous complexion.
Beloved by sentient beings, they love the Dharma that brings benefit.
Practicing a mind of loving-kindness, these lay bodhisattvas abandon all evil realms and swiftly attain rebirth in heaven.
Having attained the name of "deva," one enjoys the five sensual pleasures;
when their life in heaven comes to an end, they will ultimately not be born in the evil realms.
Reborn within the human realm, they will be born into a family of noble and wealthy lineage.
Their physical form is exceedingly sublime, such that none can deceive them.
Having nothing to guard or protect, these people practice the Dharma;
they attain vision of the supreme state and are beloved by all sentient beings.
One sleeps in peace and security, and upon waking, experiences joy and happiness;
never giving rise to fear, such a person is likewise protected by the devas.
Just as with the nature of filth and impurity, they possess this mark of contemplation.
Householders are likewise so; this extends broadly to others as well.
They shall be praised and lauded by all virtuous people;
to those who are afraid, they grant fearlessness—such are the lay bodhisattvas.
No longer serving other deities, nor beholding other deities,
this path is most upright and straight, where all the wise have gathered.
By means of these roots of goodness, one abandons all evil realms.
Possessing all-knowledge and the three insights, because he has well trained in the three precepts;
as are his meritorious deeds and as are his acts of worship,
so too should he be honored, for he is the peerless among all sentient beings.
Just as they have performed meritorious deeds, and just as they have paid homage and service,
they shall become supreme among sentient beings, just as the Buddha perceives their homage and service.
Abiding in the state of a householder, they give rise to the bodhicitta.
This praised Dharma, as well as other Dharmas, you shall now hear.
"Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva living at home should accomplish three dharmas."
What are the three?
He should distance himself from the desire for auspiciousness; this bodhisattva should maintain his dwelling by removing all obstacles and diligently cultivate extensive learning.
A bodhisattva should fulfill three dharmas and further give rise to three dharmas.
What are these three?
One should not interrupt the eloquence of a Dharma-preacher; one should diligently entreat the Dharma-preacher; and one should constantly light lamps and candles for all manner of illumination.
"One should practice these three dharmas. Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva should never, until the end of life, perform the three dharmas that constitute the conduct of a woman."
What are the three?

Not obstructing a mother so as to prevent her from hearing the Dharma; not obstructing a mother from going to where a bhikṣu is; and not forcibly detaining a wife to prevent her from reaching a bhikṣu. One who wishes to hear the Dharma does not create obstacles, nor does one abandon the right path with regard to women to commit an unrighteous act.
"If one does not perform these three dharmas, yet creates such karma, one will fall into the female state.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One should indeed offer lamps with faith again and again."
One attains the eye free from dust and defilement, as well as the attainment of the Buddha-eye.
By means of this eye, the Teacher is able to know all things;
if one knows such wisdom, then one knows true wisdom.
Knowing the dharmas of the past, and likewise those of the present,
one does not conceptualize the future, nor does one construct the three marks.
If these three marks exist, then even these three should be relinquished.
All are identical in meaning; their mutual interpenetration constitutes the absence of marks.
Regarding the various faculties taught by the Buddha, in reality, phenomena possess no such faculties.
Because they do not engage in conceptual discrimination, awakening is supreme.
Having purified the Buddha-eye, one fully perceives and understands all things;
this state is itself enlightenment, as has been described above.
The Dharma thus taught does not destroy the Dharma.
All phenomena are empty; therefore, they are called "teachings.
For those with wrong views, such as the non-Buddhists, I preach the Dharma to householders like lighting a bright lamp, so that those with eyes may perceive it.
Do not interrupt his preaching of the Dharma; within the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas, do not quickly fall into the evil realms or become one who is swiftly born blind.
Repeatedly entreat him to expound the Dharma of the Sugata.
By means of these roots of goodness, may you turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
One should not create obstacles; even if one’s mother wishes to hear the Dharma, she may appear as an extremely wicked woman, blind, hunchbacked, and utterly hideous.
Not seeing nor beholding various forms, nor hearing sublime sounds,
dwelling in a place of darkness like a snake at rest;
having created these obstacles, with greed and envy as his wife, he remains thus.
Having met a swift end to life, she became a wicked woman:
yellow-haired with blue eyes, black and hideous to behold;
her feet were afflicted with foul sores and twisted, and she was deaf, idiotic, and devoid of understanding.
In such places as these, those who lack compassion quickly receive [retribution];
being envious men, they repeatedly create the causes for desire.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
A lay bodhisattva should not perform three things. What are these three?

One should not request women for the sake of desire; one should not give ghee, clarified butter, or various other unwholesome gifts. If another wishes to leave the household life, one should not create obstacles; rather, one should encourage those who have not yet left the household life to do so. When constructing a stūpa for the Tathāgata, one should assist as a supervisor and provide guidance, and one should not seize or take away the materials belonging to it.
"These three things are what a lay bodhisattva should not do.
And he spoke in verse:
"Do not give away other women; Do not commit unrighteous acts."
Fearing that the difficulty of the obstacle of marriage might arise, he therefore gave nothing at all.
One who spoke thus went there, joined his palms in salutation, and said:
"Having given it yourself, you should give it again, with a heart of goodness and joy."
If there are few people in that monastic community, one should serve as an attendant for the Sangha;
if there is an invitation to take [food], one should assist those who are few in number.
Do not touch the water so as to make it turbid; if there are those who rely upon this [instruction], [they should act accordingly].
Without harboring resentment or malice toward them, he does not give rise to thoughts of anger or hatred.
If there are those who wish to leave the household life, including their own children and relatives,
the Bodhisattva will never create obstacles for them therein.
May all sentient beings find joy and attain the realization of nirvāṇa;
this was my original aspiration, that I might preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
Having recognized these various faults, I shall not personally harbor any envy.
"Do not dwell in constant anxiety throughout the long night, being defiled by afflictions.
Kāśyapa! Furthermore, there are three things that a lay bodhisattva should not cultivate or accumulate. What are these three?"
"Do not purchase men, do not purchase women, and do not administer poison; if there are those who do so, do not associate with them.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Abandon the practice of purchasing men, And likewise abandon the practice of purchasing women."
Do not bestow poisonous drugs; if one does so, they shall be cast away.
The devas also censure this practice, for sentient beings will encounter suffering and affliction as they wander through all directions, harmed by the arrows of grief and distress.
This brings long nights of sorrow and distress, yielding much suffering and affliction;
it may even lead to an untimely death. Therefore, one should not commit such acts.
I recognize that this fault, as well as other faults, arises from what has been done.
I shall now explain a small portion of it for the sake of awakening.
"Kāśyapa, a householder bodhisattva should not commit three things."
What are these three?
Not going to the houses of courtesans; not committing unrighteous acts with men or women; and not dwelling near a place where cattle are slaughtered.
These three things are what a lay bodhisattva should not do.
And he spoke in verse:
"One should not go to the houses of courtesans; Those who practice the foul and vile for the sake of desire Quickly incur disrespect, Because they associate with base desires."
The Teacher saw that having gone there, he would be treated with contempt by them;
he would swiftly fall into illness and, because of this, meet his end.
Whether it be a man or a woman, if they do not follow the Way, one should not associate with either.
This is what this woman does not delight in; how could one ever transgress against it?
Even if there were a place for slaughtering oxen, one would never go there;
"this is not suitable for me"—such is the Dharma of a Bodhisattva.
All such faults and afflictions, the Buddha knows them all;
therefore, regarding improper conduct, he now speaks according to reality.
That which the Buddha has thus briefly explained, we disciples are able to understand.
In the presence of the Buddha, how could one later be in vain?
Sentient beings who trust in the Noble One desire to reach Nirvana swiftly;
it is for their sake that I speak these words, not for those who are difficult to instruct.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva should accomplish three dharmas.
What are these three?

While dwelling at home, he regards it as if he were a guest and does not conceive the notion of "mine. Regarding what has already been given away, he conceives the notion of a mere accumulation; regarding what has not yet been given away, he maintains the notion that it is a thousand yojanas distant from him. He does not conceive the notion of hoarding or storing up treasures for the sake of his children.
“Kāśyapa! A lay bodhisattva should accomplish these three perceptions.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One should cultivate the perception of death: 'I shall not live long.
Therefore, whatever treasures one has stored away, these riches should be made firm through practice.
This is for the sake of distinguishing between men and women; it is never for the sake of profit."
Swiftly seek the steadfast Dharma; regarding body, life, and wealth, one should desire enlightenment with earnest gravity. One’s actions should not be frivolous;
for the sake of seeking the benefits of the Dharma, one must subdue all [afflictions] at all times.
Like the play of a young girl, or like light gradually appearing,
one who delights not in attachment to flavors is thus in the Dharma of desire.
Reading and reciting without rest, they are adorned with the excellent Dharma.
It is difficult to cultivate and assemble among the various multitudes.
Such similar dharmas as these, O Kāśyapa, I have already explained;
those who are wise and sharp, I know them all.
"Having known and understood this, he feels compassion for himself;
at that time, such a person will encounter me again and again. "Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
A lay bodhisattva who accomplishes three dharmas does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What are these three? They are:

transforming parents who lack faith so that they abide in faith; exhorting parents who violate the precepts so that they abide in the precepts; and exhorting parents who are stingy and greedy so that they abide in renunciation. Furthermore, they praise the unsurpassed path and expound the Dharma amidst the great assembly.
This is called the first dharma by which a lay bodhisattva does not regress from the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a lay bodhisattva should skillfully know those who are worthy of offerings and those who are not. Having known this, they should provide food and offerings to those who are worthy, while not providing them to those who are not; furthermore, they should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all such persons.
Kāśyapa! This is called the second dharma by which a lay bodhisattva does not regress from the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

Whatever wealth a lay bodhisattva has acquired through diligent toil, they should not lose it, nor allow it to be entirely exhausted, nor give it away to others. They should store it securely and firmly, bestowing it upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who abide in pure precepts, granting them equal fiefs and material endowments that are free from attachment for the sake of all those of pure conduct.
"Kāśyapa! This is called the third dharma by which a lay bodhisattva does not retreat from the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
And he spoke in verse:
"If a lay bodhisattva, seeking to gather unsurpassed bodhi,
gives rise to the three kinds of wisdom and trains in the unsurpassed path;
yet if their father and mother possess evil wisdom and lack faith,"
I exhort them to give rise to faith, And cause them to incline toward the sublime Dharma.

For those who are stingy, I urge them to abandon their transgressions and abide in the precepts; For those lacking wisdom, I urge them to cultivate faith and wisdom, Directing them toward unsurpassed bodhi, Exhorting them to reach this state.
If one travels to the four quarters seeking those who preach the Dharma well,
one should practice the gift of the Dharma to increase wisdom.
One should teach those who violate the precepts to abide in the precepts, and teach those without faith to have faith.
One who lacks wisdom should be taught wisdom; such a person will never fall back.
If one sees a wise bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and is learned, one should respectfully approach and draw near to them, consulting them again and again.
Therefore, by associating with bhikṣus, repeatedly consulting them, and swiftly receiving their teaching, one does not fall back.
Thus, their awakening-wisdom increases; this is the place of hearing and the way of the wise.
Once awakened wisdom has been increased, one gives even one's own flesh as an offering.
This is the mark of faith and resolve, as I have described it;
for one who lacks a faithful mind cannot advance toward Bodhi.
Gradually one sees increase, and swiftly attains growth;
thus, for all these increases, they will not be difficult to obtain.
Having understood this increase, whether for oneself or for others,
With a joyful heart they approach; such people increase their wisdom.
Whatever wealth and possessions they have gathered, all those who observe the precepts place before them.
He speaks no words of discord, nor ever utters divergent speech;
being steadfast, valiant, and firm in giving, he is one who can realize the state of a Tathāgata.
Gentle and easy to dwell with, the courageous one attains loving-kindness.
With joy, he relinquishes firmly; as it was before, so it is afterward.
This courageous and supreme donor does not seek from others;
the most steadfast among all givers, there is nothing he will not give away.
If one has previously offered gold, silver, and coins,
and now aspires to the supreme Dharma— the most profound and highest phrases—
then all devas and the world will accord with and single-mindedly make offerings to them.
Those who seek the Dharma should all make offerings to such a person.
The courageous one gathers the Dharma and sustains his life through the Dharma;
possessing the supreme Dharma of wisdom, he shall become a savior of the world.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there are three dharmas for a lay bodhisattva who, having set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, quickly falls back into the stage of a śrāvaka and enters parinirvāṇa.
What are the three?

If, having once briefly generated the bodhicitta, one fears the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals, and conceives of this path to enlightenment as a heavy burden, seeking various roots of goodness without focused reflection and without taking pleasure in seeking them well—such a person is harmed by their own mind and gives rise to the perception of suffering.
Kāśyapa! This is called the first dharma by which a lay bodhisattva regresses from the unsurpassed path and quickly falls to the level of a śrāvaka and enters parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

If a lay bodhisattva, having once briefly generated the mind of enlightenment, gives a gift while harboring anger, and feels regret after having given it, this person will not be able to reach the wisdom of a Buddha.
Kāśyapa! These are the two dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva regresses from the mind of enlightenment and swiftly falls into the stage of a śrāvaka, attaining parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

If a lay bodhisattva, having once briefly aroused the mind of enlightenment, does not apply diligent effort to accumulate extensive learning, that person will, by means of these few roots of goodness, quickly enter nirvana.
“Kāśyapa! These are called the three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva regresses from the mind of enlightenment.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Having generated the bodhicitta, if one does not cultivate correct practice,
one ruins the Buddha-vehicle and falls into the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
Bodhi is not attained by those who lack faith, nor by those who are indolent."
Those who are stingy, greedy, and lack wisdom create obstacles for themselves.
Those who recognize kindness, abide in pure precepts, and always delight in the practice of relinquishment—
finding joy in their hearts when giving— will find that awakening is not difficult to attain.
The mind creates all evils, and the mind can also practice giving;
if this mind of sentient beings is firm, it shall become a stūpa for the world.
If one does not abandon these dharmas, the mind will incline toward bodhi.
"When he attains Buddhahood and appears in the world, he shall serve as a field of merit for the world. Kāśyapa!
There are three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva regresses from the mind of enlightenment and falls into the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha, thereby entering parinirvāṇa."
What are these three?
They are when a lay bodhisattva, having once generated the resolve for awakening, becomes stingy and secretive regarding the secret Dharma. Kāśyapa!
This is called the first way in which a lay bodhisattva regresses from the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) and falls into the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha,
thereby passing into parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
once a lay bodhisattva has generated the thought of enlightenment, they look forward to an auspicious time and seek out a favorable day.
Kāśyapa! These are called the two dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva retreats from the mind of enlightenment and falls into the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha, attaining parinirvāṇa therein.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
A lay bodhisattva who is indolent and lazy does not diligently seek the dharmas that assist in awakening.
Kāśyapa! These are called the three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva retreats from the mind of awakening and falls into the nirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha, attaining parinirvāṇa therein.
And he spoke in verse:
"One who is stingy and begrudges the secret Dharma, failing to instruct others, shall fall into the stage of a Pratyekabuddha; this is a falling away from Bodhi."
This leads to falling back into the three [realms], where loss of benefit brings suffering;
having departed from the present, one harbors doubt regarding Bodhi.
Having contemplated the Mahāyāna, one should swiftly aspire for auspiciousness.
This is not the mark of one resolved through faith; the Buddha does not associate with such.
If there is one with extreme single-mindedness who steadfastly seeks the path to Bodhi, they shall pay no homage to others, except for the stupas of the world.
If one possesses such faith, one shall not seek other deities;
this is the supreme accomplishment, called the God among Gods.
Once the bodhicitta has been generated, one shall not pay homage to others.
This is the supreme form, found in every place of rebirth.
"Kāśyapa! There are three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva acquires an extremely dark body."
What are these three dharmas?

Extinguishing the lamps lit within a Buddhist stūpa; giving rise to a mind of anger when others are engaged in a dispute; and interfering in the disputes of others in matters that do not concern oneself; and seeing a person of dark complexion and reviling them for their appearance.
“Kāśyapa! These are called the three dharmas by which the body of a lay bodhisattva becomes utterly black.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Lighting a lamp within a stūpa, he seized that radiance;
his body was exceedingly black, like a lacquer tray.
Seeing the black-skinned form, he reviled him, saying: 'I am white, and you are utterly black.'"
Having thus disparaged others, one receives a body black as charcoal.
One who well guards the karma of speech does not lose the results of the deeds they have performed;
according to the deeds one has committed, such will be the vessel one shall possess.
“Kāśyapa! There are three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva is born into a family of artisans.
What are the three?
Kāśyapa! Suppose a lay bodhisattva has personally received the five precepts, yet when a friend comes from afar, they give them alcohol to drink, or invites others to drink alcohol with them.
Kāśyapa! This is called the first dharma by which a lay bodhisattva is born into a family of artisans.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Kāśyapa, a lay bodhisattva who maintains pure conduct for himself but incites others to engage in lustful and defiled acts will, because of this karma, be born into a family of artisans.
These are called the two dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva is born into a family of artisans.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,

if a lay bodhisattva sees another person performing religious rites or diligently engaged in recitation and study, yet that person intends to build a dwelling for the gods, the bodhisattva says this to them:
"Abandon your recitation and study; engage in manual labor, and once that work is finished, return to your studies.
Because of this karma, he was born into a family of artisans.
He then spoke in verse:
"To invite others with wine, as well as one's own acquaintances,
and to offer wine as the primary hospitality— this karma leads to rebirth among the artisans.
One will be unable to work with knives, needles, or any other craft."
Having merely sat upon the ground, he held a bellows in his hands.
Having abandoned women himself, he praised sexual desire to others;
by the karmic retribution of this deed, he was born into a family of craftsmen.
Unable to forge knives or needles, and ignorant of how to beat the bellows,
he was ordered to grasp the hammer to forge iron nails.
By creating such obstacles to the Dharma, he caused others to abandon the Dharma.
Falling into the house of artisans, this person is born into such a family.
There they see no bellows, nor do they see hammers or tongs;
all the various tools are broken—such is the retribution for their karma.
Kāśyapa! Guard your verbal karma, and likewise guard and be cautious regarding mental karma; do not speak of any unwholesome dharmas to others.
One undergoes manifold sufferings within birth and death; once born, craving increases.
"Therefore, one should diligently practice the Dharma and abandon all unwholesome dharmas.

Kāśyapa, when a lay bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, he is born into a royal family with a complexion that is exceptionally beautiful, upright, and lovely— vivid, pure, red and white— and he is neither indolent nor dull-witted, but is wise and discerning."
What are the three? Kāśyapa!
When a lay bodhisattva beholds a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa never seen before, and having seen them, gives rise to a mind of faith and reverence:
Thinking, "This is a field of merit; this one should be honored; this one should be revered;
this is a field of merit," and having thus conceived faith and respect, they invite them to accept robes, food and drink, bedding, and various medicines for illness.
Kāśyapa! This is called the first dharma by which a lay bodhisattva is born into a royal family.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
A lay bodhisattva remains steadfastly established in their original vow; while abiding in that vow, they dwell according to what they have spoken and never utter falsehoods.
Kāśyapa, these are called the two dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva is born into a royal family.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
a lay bodhisattva should approach and consult with śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who abide in pure precepts, and cultivate the firm Dharma.
“Kāśyapa! These are called the three dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva is born into the family of a great king.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The wise one, having seen and known, and the one of pure precepts and great learning,
gives rise to such a thought and goes there to invite him.
Once he has been invited, he acts exactly as required."
This is not for the sake of nirvāṇa; in what is bestowed, there is no harm.
This is the grasping of the firm Dharma; like those whom one draws near to, various wisdoms increase, and that which is difficult to obtain is swiftly acquired.
For one with such faith who is intent upon awakening,
awakening is not difficult to attain, just as it is for the path of the wise.
Having lived the most excellent life, they renounce the most excellent wealth and possessions.
Having gathered the most sublime Dharma, one realizes the supreme cessation.
Such a person is born into a noble lineage; possessing the most sublime form, wearing the most sublime robes, they attain the highest Nirvana.
One who understands such a Dharma, a person of wisdom and intelligence,
practices without timidity as taught by the Buddha.
With their resolve directed toward the Supreme Vehicle, such a person reaches that Supreme Vehicle.
All fetters and latent tendencies are extinguished, Just like that supreme fruit.
As the karma one has created, So too is its retribution;
It never perishes from beginning to end, Even throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas.

“Kāśyapa! A lay bodhisattva dwelling on the stage of a householder who accomplishes three dharmas plants these roots of goodness and will never again experience the pleasures of the five desires, until finally attaining the unsurpassed right path.”

Kāśyapa! A lay bodhisattva who upholds the five precepts does not praise the pleasures of the five desires to others, nor does he entice women; he diligently cultivates his own practice, giving rise to this thought:
"I shall not now draw near to women; I have no desire for the pleasures of the five senses until I have attained the unsurpassed Right Path."
"Kāśyapa! This is called the first dharma for a lay bodhisattva: never to accept the pleasures of the five desires until one attains the realization of the unsurpassed right path."
Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
if a lay bodhisattva hears such profound sūtras as these and practices them with pure faith, Kāśyapa!
If there are those who are not yet fit vessels for these profound sutras, one should instead encourage them [toward other teachings]. Kāśyapa!

If a son of good family can cause others to abandon their doubts, that bodhisattva, by virtue of these roots of goodness, will attain unimpeded eloquence and unattached eloquence; from birth until the end of life, he will swiftly behold the Buddhas, and after his death, he will be reborn in the heavens, before long attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa! These are called the two dharmas of a lay bodhisattva, by which they eventually attain the unsurpassed right path and do not experience the five desires.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

All the roots of goodness possessed by a lay bodhisattva are dedicated entirely toward the unsurpassed right path; they take no pleasure in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; they take no pleasure in wealth or rank, take no pleasure in sovereignty, and take no pleasure in retinues. With an untainted mind and untainted retribution, they swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and do not accept the pleasures of the five desires.
Kāśyapa! These are called the three dharmas of a lay bodhisattva: by not greedily grasping at the pleasures of the five desires, they shall even attain the realization of the unsurpassed right path.
And he spoke in verse:
“Living at home, one observes the five precepts, Maintaining and guarding them well;
One stays far from associating with women, And despises this lowly state.”
Such are the corresponding dharmas, which cultivate and accumulate the fulfillment of the outflows-free.
If there are those who harbor doubts, they are taught so that they may quickly attain understanding;
all roots of goodness are entirely dedicated toward Bodhi.
By means of these roots of goodness, may they swiftly renounce the pleasures of the five desires;
may they always possess extensive learning and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
may they give rise to the mind of great compassion and seek the path to Bodhi.
"Therefore, having heard this, one should give rise to noble, virtuous, and sublime desire;
never again associating with sensual desires, one shall swiftly turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what name should this Dharma of the sutra be known?
How shall we together receive and uphold it?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“This sutra is titled ‘The Exposition of the Threefold Precepts,’ it is also titled ‘The Proclamation of the Bodhisattva’s Prohibitory Precepts,’ and it is also titled ‘The Collection of All Buddha-Dharmas.’”

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy.
The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Threefold Precepts, Scroll II.
